news.title: 'Defeated Goliath': Did faith help Democrats flip key midterm races?
news.text:
As Democrat James Talarico of Texas delivered his acceptance speech Tuesday in Austin after his decisive U.S. Senate race win over Republican Ken Paxton, a large placard in front of him featured the words, “Love Thy Neighbor.”

That message seemed to resonate with voters nationwide, who vastly backed Democrats in a sweeping series of victories that some saw as a humanitarian rejection of federal policies such as overly aggressive immigration enforcement, unauthorized war, efforts to stamp out diversity and economic measures that have left many families struggling.

Religion proved pivotal at the ballot box nationwide, experts say, shaping voter views on key issues that turned previously red states blue. Faith was also brandished by candidates like Talarico to appeal to the electorate, even as conservatives blasted his progressive Christianity; in some cases, religion was weaponized by opponents, as in Islamophobic attacks and ad campaigns in Michigan and Texas.

“You did see some rejection of Republicans, especially with Hispanic Catholics in Texas,” said Michael Moreland, director of the Eleanor H. McCullen Center for Law, Religion and Public Policy at Villanova University in Pennsylvania. “Especially along the South Texas border, aspects of the administration’s immigration enforcement alienated a lot of voters. President Trump in 2024 peeled off a lot of those voters, but he lost them Tuesday night.”

Democrat megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Kansas, while in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton was elected both the state’s first Jewish and female governor, her Judaism informing her progressive platform.

Meanwhile, a record seven Muslims were elected to Congress nationwide, including Democrat physician Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, who became the nation’s first Muslim U.S. senator. The number could rise to eight, depending on how California Democrat Aisha Wahab fares in her race for the state’s 14th Congressional district seat.

Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian and grandson of a Baptist preacher, was among several candidates who charted rare territory for white Democrats by making religion a central part of his campaign, citing scripture and stressing his Biblical grounding.

Dubbed “Talafreako” by President Donald Trump, Talarico kicked off his acceptance speech by using the Bible story of David and Goliath as a metaphor for his race against Paxton and “billionaire megadonors” like Elon Musk, who spent nearly $230 million to support Paxton’s campaign against Talarico.

“We went up against our own Goliath – the richest man in the world, the most powerful man in the world and the entire D.C. establishment,” Talarico said. Comparing himself to the shepherd boy who wielded a slingshot to slay his mightier foe, he told the crowd: “You were my slingshot. The people of Texas were my slingshot. And tonight, we defeated Goliath.”

Swing to Dems more pronounced among some faiths

Nationwide, exit polls conducted by NBC News revealed sizable shifts among several groups in the midterms compared to the 2024 election. Just under half of Catholics backed Republican candidates in the midterms, NBC found, compared to 59% who voted for Trump in 2024.

Jewish voters, meanwhile, swung the other way, NBC found: While 78% supported Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in 2024, 68% voted for Democrats in this year’s midterms.

"Donald Trump said voters should pretend he was on the ballot in the midterms, and Jewish Americans did just that," Halie Soifer, CEO of the Jewish Democratic Council of America, said in a statement. "Jewish voters are not a monolith, but they widely disapprove of Donald Trump. This, coupled with the strength of the Democratic candidates who flipped red seats blue, led to overwhelming support for Democrats among Jewish voters in this election.”

Among religiously unaffiliated voters, NBC found, 27% supported Trump in 2024, compared to 20% who favored Republican candidates this fall.

Meanwhile, 86% of Muslims supported Democratic candidates in 2026 – the share wasn’t tallied in 2024 – while slightly fewer Protestants or other Christians supported Republican candidates this year compared with 2024.

Exit polls conducted by the Council on American-Islamic Relations indicated the Iran war, the economy, rising Islamophobia and Israel’s war in Gaza were foremost in their midterm voting choices. “Rising Islamophobia strengthened their motivation to vote,” the council said in a statement. “They overwhelmingly backed Democrats, but many remain unconvinced that either party listens to their concerns.”

During his race for Michigan’s Senate seat, El-Sayed was dismissed as a “jihadist” by Trump and accused of links to terrorist groups, both without evidence. Others criticized him for what they saw as a failure to sufficiently denounce antisemitism.

Frank Lacopo, an assistant professor of history at Southeast Missouri State University in Cape Girardeau, said such comments backfired with voters concerned with other issues.

“It really seems like El-Sayed’s more secular messaging on affordability was more effective,” Lacopo said. “What he showed people in Michigan was a vision of an American who happens to be Muslim.”

Did Catholics feel betrayed by Trump, GOP?

More than 50 million Catholics live in the U.S., with about 53% identifying as Republican, according to the Pew Research Center. Accounting for about a quarter of U.S. voters, they represent a broad political spectrum.

“It’s hard to neatly categorize the Catholic vote, because it depends on other factors – whether they’re white Catholics, Hispanic Catholics, young Catholics or more churchgoing ones,” Moreland said.

Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of Catholic Vote, a conservative political advocacy organization based in Carmel, Indiana, said Catholics’ midterm swing toward Democrats reflected the broad concerns of the American electorate.

“In this election, Catholics are representative of the American population writ large,” Reinhardt said. “They care about necessities. The socioeconomic stratosphere of Catholics is pretty ordinary.”

In 2024, she said, Catholic voters largely believed Trump would be a greater arbiter of Catholic values. This time around, some may have felt betrayed by Trump’s broken anti-war promises, while anti-abortion advocates likely felt the president hasn’t done enough to advance their cause.

“The Catholic vote is soft Republican when there’s a Republican who advances their ideals,” Reinhardt said. “But they swing back when they feel their values are not being met. The Iran war was a factor too, but I’m not sure whether it’s an issue because it was declared immoral by the pope or because people didn’t want a forever war.”

Catholic concerns loomed large at the state level, such as in Virginia, where local bishops led a furious campaign that unsuccessfully sought to mobilize voters to reject ballot measures expanding abortion rights and removing wordage in the state constitution strictly defining marriage as between a man and woman.

“That was one where Catholics were heroic in their efforts,” Reinhardt said. “But 700,000 Catholics in Virginia won’t overturn the majority there.”

Lacopo thinks a factor that may have been a factor in Catholics’ Democratic swing is the Catholic church’s growing presence online.

“It’s important not to underestimate the power that Catholic church messaging on social media has on Catholics,” he said. “Even if they’re not practicing Catholics. A lot of Americans began to subscribe to Vatican News when Leo became pope, and they identify with him as an American.”

Pope Leo XIV’s fluency in both English and Spanish allows him to reach a wide swath of voters, he said. Meanwhile, the pope’s social media features a constant feed of direct quotes from the Chicago-born pontiff that help American followers see him as someone representing “a more accepting, open-arms version of Christianity.”

In general, Lacopo feels Democrats fielded better quality candidates who appealed to voters, with faith part of the package in states like Texas and Kansas.

“Talarico was absolutely perfect as a candidate for Texas because he had a way of speaking that came from his background of training as a Presbyterian minister,” Lacopo said. “He was able to use Christian messaging in a way that couldn’t be countered by Republicans.”

He noted Talarico’s acceptance speech also focused on what many consider the central tenets of Christian teaching, the notion of loving God and one’s neighbor – a message he thinks resonated not just with Texas Latinos anxious over immigration policy but with the kind of voters who plant signs reading “No Human Being is Illegal” in their front yards.

“I’m surprised and not surprised at the same time that Democrats have taken so long to latch on to that,” Lacopo said. “Even if you’re a secular voter and don’t practice religion, you can relate to the second part of that message.”

news.title: Reporting the ideas at the center of our political moment
news.text:
As I write this, the Monitor’s national news desk is scrambling to cover the aftermath of the Democratic wave in the U.S. midterm elections. Our reporters have crisscrossed the country – from Michigan to Texas, California to Maine – to talk with voters, policymakers, and candidates. Our goal is to not simply document the winners and losers, but to try to better understand the big ideas shaping the country, and to find those glimmers of compromise and shared values that might lay the foundation for civil and effective governance.

Our latest in political reporting is on our website – please take a look.

In this issue, we delve into a subject that was at the core of this recent election – and has, according to much research, undermined the confidence of many Americans in their government.

In May of this year, Politico and Public First found that 80% of 2024 Kamala Harris voters and 77% of Donald Trump voters agreed with the statement: “There is too much money in American politics.”

A YouGov poll from last year found that 76% of Americans (84 % of Democrats, 68% of Republicans, and 77% of independents) agreed that the “appearance of wealthy donors or corporations gaining influence over or access to elected officials causes me to lose faith in this democracy.”

I first reached out to Jeffrey Winters, a political science professor at Northwestern University, after I heard him talk about his recent book, “The Blind Spot: How Oligarchs Dominate Our Democracy.”

I was struck by his argument that oligarchy is structurally baked into our political system. But I was even more taken by his lack of partisanship, and the calm, historically minded, and above-the-fray approach he took to an issue that is riling both sides of the political aisle. I found myself thinking of his work repeatedly as I read about the midterms – including our reporting about artificial intelligence companies pouring funds into both Democratic and Republican campaigns.

(Dr. Winters urged me not to call these funds “donations.” They are, he told me, “political investments.”)

You can read his piece on page 25. It is the second installment of our new “terms” essays – writings by scholars and thinkers on common words that have a rich history and nuance worthy of exploration.

If you missed Harry Boyte and Trygve Throntveit’s essay, “Reclaiming citizenship,” which ran in the Nov. 2 issue, check it out on our website. You’ll find it under “What does citizenship mean? A case for a broader definition.” And if you have suggestions for a term that you think deserves a deep dive, please get in touch.
news.summary: Our reporting delves into the ideas underlying our political moment. In this issue of the magazine, we explore the concept of American oligarchy.
news.author: Stephanie Hanes

news.title: Anthony Constantino’s Post-Election Crashout
news.text:
At an election eve rally in upstate New York, Republican congressional candidate Anthony Constantino told the crowd he had a dramatic announcement: Donald Trump was wrong about one thing. An audible gasp rippled through the converted airplane hangar. What could it possibly be? 

“Fake news” wasn’t accurate, Constantino said. “It’s actually evil news.” 

The candidate went on to gesture at the press pen and tell the crowd to take photos of its nefarious inhabitants. The campaign had not granted me credentials, so, like everyone else, I turned my attention to the people Constantino said “should be ashamed” of themselves. What Constantino did not seem to realize was that the most embarrassing thing about the event was that it was happening at all.

One day before the midterms, JD Vance and Donald Trump Jr. were flying into a district the president won by more than 20 points in 2024. Polls showed the race as a dead heat, despite Constantino loaning his campaign $17 million of the fortune he amassed through his novelty company Sticker Mule. Vance and Trump Jr., who arrived on Air Force Two accompanied by the soundtrack of Top Gun, were the reinforcements. 

So, too, was Carol Constantino, who introduced her 44-year-old son as a once challenging kid who nevertheless deserved Republicans’ support. “I’ll also admit that Anthony wasn’t easy,” Carol said about what he was like after her husband passed away when Anthony was a boy. “He was a challenge at times. He was stubborn.”

On Tuesday, Constantino won New York’s 21st congressional district, which runs from around Albany up to the Canadian border, by about 2 points. It was an abysmal showing considering that Rep. Elise Stefanik carried the district by 24 points in 2024. In typical fashion, Constantino showed no humility. Instead, he celebrated his victory with the venom that marked his campaign from start to finish. Come January, Constantino, who will be one of just two GOP freshmen from the Northeast in the new Congress, is in pole position to be the much diminished Republican caucus’ most uncontrollable loudmouth. 

As I wrote in a profile earlier this year, Constantino prevailed over the New York GOP establishment in his primary thanks to a Trump endorsement and millions of dollars of his money. He is one of the most unusual candidates I have ever covered. In addition to being a sticker mogul, Constantino has moonlighted as a rapper and stand-up comic. (Example: A bit about Kamala Harris supporters vomiting before and after he put his penis in their mouths.) He also spent much of the past decade living in Mexico pursuing a new career as a technically professional boxer. 

Stefanik is a Harvard graduate who in 2014 became the youngest woman ever elected to Congress. Despite attending Albany Academy at the same time, she and Constantino have radically different public images. As I’ve written : 

During his campaign launch held in front of a wall of free turkeys, Constantino labeled Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez a “perra falsa”—Spanish for fake bitch. He told Gerard Kassar, the head of New York’s Conservative Party, to get “his ass” in a boxing ring, so he could punch him “in the fucking face legally.” In the video for his Zohran Mamdani diss track—which includes the line “fuck you bitch” and includes a reference to the New York mayor’s “boy Osama”—he makes a throat-slitting gesture. In keeping with this thuggish persona, Constantino’s close associates have been accused or found guilty of kidnapping, stealing money from a youth baseball league, and lying to Congress. 

On election night, Constantino rambled for nearly 30 minutes, while wearing a Mike Amiri trucker hat that retails for nearly $400. He thanked his campaign adviser Roger Stone, who Constantino said had told him to be nicer during the campaign. (That may be a first for Stone, a convicted felon and infamous, self-proclaimed “dirty trickster.”) He then had his buddy Jason “Greatness” Jensen—a face-tattooed white man who plays an important role in the Constantino cinematic universe—do a brief rap: “He backed by God, plus he Trump-endorsed.” (God’s position in the race could not be verified.)

As the remarks continued, Constantino increasingly resembled the difficult boy his mom had mentioned raising at the previous day’s rally. He blamed the press for his failure to win by the 20-point margin he’d wanted. The reporters who covered him were “scumbags” and a “bunch of fucking assholes.” Even the members of the press who weren’t “bad people,” were “evil” for failing to expose their colleagues. Pointing to a reporter, he continued, “Look at that asshole, right there … Take a picture of him … [City & State reporter] Kate Lisa, another fucking asshole.”

From there, he had one of those reporters kicked out of the event. “He’s so angry right now, you can just see it in his eyes,” Constantino said in what came across as textbook projection. “He’s just a angry motherfucker,” the congressman elect later added. As a reminder, this was a victory speech. It is hard to imagine what a concession speech might have sounded like. By way of a closing message, he said that Trump should consider “freeing” Sean Combs, the hip-hop mogul known as “Diddy” who was convicted last year of transporting people across state lines for prostitution.

Constantino’s invective was not limited to the stage. Around 3:15 a.m. on election night, Constantino sent a text message to Schenectady County GOP Chair Liz Joy that stated, “Resign you scumbag.” (Joy shared the screenshot on X.) About 10 minutes later, the congressman elect posted on X that “NY-21 Republican Chairs are objectively a group of scammers,” adding that Bruce Blakeman, the defeated GOP nominee for New York governor, “was in on the con.” 

In a public reply on Thursday, Blakeman called Constantino “by far the worst candidate I ever encountered.” He is not alone in the assessment; the editorial board of the Albany Times Union wrote in June that it could not “recall ever meeting a more unsuitable candidate.” 

Constantino’s post-victory crashout continued into Friday, when he wrote that a female New York reporter is “33 and looks 53.” When an X user who goes by the name JohnsCow (follower count: 7) called Constantino “Low IQ,” Constantino replied at 2:02 a.m., “My IQ is 132.”

After the rally on Monday, I headed over to the press area to talk to a fellow member of the “evil news” whom I recognized from attacks posted on Constantino’s X feed. But our conversation was cut short by a surreal scene: Constantino was rolling past us on a mobility scooter with a white-bearded veteran more or less sitting on his lap. Moving silently across the floor of the old hangar, the candidate finally seemed to be having a good time.

He had just one question for his staff: “Where’s my mom?”

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: DC Workers Pay For Ridiculous Amount Of Porn On Job, GPS Data Suggests
news.text:
People in Washington, D.C., consume pornography on OnlyFans at high rates during the workday, according to Max Anderson, CEO of OnlyFinder, whose company published a report on OnlyFans spending.

People in the nation’s capital spend more on OnlyFans content per capita than any of the 50 states in the US, according to the OnlyFinder’s OnlyFans Wrapped 2026 report. OnlyFans spending in the District drops off heavily at night, suggesting commuters consume a disproportionate amount of pornographic content during the workday, Anderson told the Daily Caller News Foundation. 

While the public report does not present data related to the time spent on OnlyFans, Anderson explained the firm’s internal finding about pornography spending in the District to the DCNF. 

“People who work in D.C. are heavily using OnlyFans inside the boundaries of the District of Columbia during the workday, and then their usage drops off a cliff when they go home to the suburbs at night,” Anderson told the DCNF. 

“The data certainly supports that D.C. workers are heavily using OnlyFans during the workday,” Anderson told the DCNF.

OnlyFinder is an online service that works as a search engine and discovery tool for OnlyFans content. OnlyFans does not have a curated homepage or search feature embedded on the website, so most internet traffic searching for OnlyFans content is routed through OnlyFinder, according to Anderson. OnlyFinder began reporting the estimated spending on OnlyFans content in 2025. 

The population of D.C. spends $277,248.85 per 10,000 adults on OnlyFans content, OnlyFinder report estimates by tracking the geographic location of devices engaging with the site’s content. 

Around 23% of D.C. jobs are in the federal government, and federal workers have previously come under fire for watching porn on the job in a 2017 investigation from NBC News 4. The investigation alleged that over 100 federal workers were sifting through pornography for up to six hours a day on their office computers.

OnlyFans is a UK-based subscription service platform used almost exclusively for pornography and not-safe-for-work content. Subscribers pay a monthly fee to access content from producers, but per Anderson, a significant portion of subscriber spending is on pay-per-view personalized content and direct messaging. (RELATED: Chinese-Linked Network Of More Than 400 AI Apps Hid Deepfake Porn Tools From Apple, Google)

The United States is the largest market for OnlyFans, with Americans spending $4.9 billion on the platform in 2026, per the OnlyFinder report. People in the Portland, Oregon, greater metropolitan area spent $459,994.20 per 10,000 adults on OnlyFans, more than any other metro area in the world. 

States that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election spent about 13% more on OnlyFans per capita than states that President Donald Trump won. The top 12 states for per capita OnlyFans spending were all Democrat-led states. 

Over 90% of OnlyFans spenders are men, Anderson said. Men report feeling lonelier than ever, and 90% of men consume pornography at least once a month, according to a study published by the National Institutes of Health.
news.summary: ‘During the workday’

news.title: Could Trump's Home State Flip in 2028? What Democrats' Florida Results Show
news.text: Florida largely resisted the Democratic wave that swept across the country in the midterms, but with several congressional races shifting in Democrats’ favor as opposed to the last midterm election in 2022, the results are raising questions about whether the state could become more competitive in 2028. While Republicans have celebrated Florida’s ability to remain largely red during the nationwide blue wave this week, the results tell a more complicated story. A post-election memo from Governor-elect Byron Donalds’ campaign called Florida the “premier Republican stronghold in America” now that Texas’ gubernatorial seat was won by Democrat Gina Hinojosa. Despite Republicans winning most of Florida’s congressional races, many shifted toward Democrats compared with the 2022 midterms, sometimes by significant margins. Florida carries particular significance for President Donald Trump, who has made the state his primary residence since leaving New York and has seen it become increasingly Republican in recent elections. Trump won Florida by roughly 13 points over Kamala Harris in 2024, a dramatic shift from 2016, when he carried the state by just over 1 point. How Close Were Florida Midterm Races? Republicans had a narrow victory over their Democratic opponents in many congressional races, including the special election for the U.S. Senate seat and in several House races, with four races still too close to call. Florida Republicans had hoped to grow their congressional majority after DeSantis pushed through a mid-decade redistricting plan that reshaped several Democratic-held seats in the GOP’s favor. But despite the new map, Republicans failed to immediately flip any of the targeted Democratic seats, leaving the party without the congressional gains it had sought from redistricting. However, DeSantis said that had the congressional map not been changed, Democrats might have flipped several Republican-held seats in Florida. “In 2024 Florida voters sent 20 Republicans and 8 Democrats to the US House. In April 2026, Florida enacted a revised map to unwind an unconstitutional racial gerrymander,” DeSantis posted on X after the midterms. “Last night, Florida voters likely elected 20 Republicans and 8 Democrats to the US House. Had the old map been in effect, it would have been 18 Republicans and 10 Democrats.” U.S. Senate Results A special election was held for the U.S. Senate seat to complete the remainder of former Senator Marco Rubio’s term, considering he left the seat to serve as Trump’s Secretary of State. Republican Ashley Moody, who was appointed to replace Rubio in 2025, won the Senate election during this week’s midterms over her Democratic challenger Angie Nixon by less than 3 percentage points. Moody received 50.9 percent of the vote compared to Nixon’s 48 percent. In 2022, Rubio, who was the Republican incumbent at the time, won the seat by more than 16 points over his Democratic challenger Val Demings. Nixon’s three-point loss comes even as she didn’t receive funding from the Senate Majority PAC or the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Nixon previously told Newsweek that she was “not getting massive amounts of money from ultra-wealthy billionaires, from these big major corporations,” despite support for her campaign from other political players like Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, among others. That lack of major corporate funding raises another question: With more financial backing, could a Democrat win Florida’s U.S. Senate seat? “I think Democrats are encouraged by Texas' election outcome and are preparing for 2028,” University of Florida political science professor Sharon Wright Austin told Newsweek on Friday. “Some candidates only lost by small margins. Mid decade redistricting also backfired because Democratic incumbents won despite it. We have to question whether [Democratic gubernatorial candidate David] Jolly or Nixon could've won if the national Democratic party had devoted more funds to their campaign.” Florida Governor’s Race Donalds won the gubernatorial election, becoming Florida’s first Black governor after receiving 50 percent of the vote compared to his Democratic challenger David Jolly’s 48.7 percent. However, the competitive race was a change from the last gubernatorial election held in 2022, when then-incumbent Republican Ron DeSantis, who was term-limited this year, won his re-election bid by nearly 20 points. Following the midterms, DeSantis issued a dire prediction for Republicans, saying the party might not win its congressional majority back in 2028 but should instead look to 2032 Senate control. “Dems will get 55 Senate seats and 250+ House seats," he posted on X on Wednesday. "Looking at the Senate map and considering such a massive House margin, it is very unlikely Republicans will recapture the Congress in 2028. Might not have a shot at Senate control until 2032.” U.S. House Race U.S. House races in Florida, while many were retained by Republicans, also saw significantly different margins than in the last midterms. Notable shifts include District 13, held by Republican Anna Paulina Luna, who won her re-election bid by only eight-tenths of a point this year, compared with 2022, when she first won the seat by 8 points over her Democratic challenger. In District 21, Republican incumbent Brian Mast won his re-election bid by 9 points over his Democratic challenger James Martin. While not a narrow victory, Mast’s margin was much higher in 2022, when he won by 27 points. Republicans also made gains over their 2022 midterm performance in some U.S. House races. For example, Democrat Pia Dandiya won District 22 by just under 4 percentage points over her Republican opponent Casey Askar this year, whereas Democrats secured the seat by 10 points in 2022. Four House races remain too close to call. They include District 7, where Republican Ryan Elijah leads Democrat Bale Dalton by half a percentage point. Republicans flipped the seat during the 2022 midterm elections. In District 9, Democrat incumbent Darren Soto is leading his Republican challenger Dan Green by little over half a percentage point. This is a race where Republicans have made gains, as Soto won his re-election bid in the 2022 midterms by over 7 percentage points. In District 26, only 0.8 percentage points separate Republican incumbent Mario Diaz-Balart from his Democratic challenger Nicole Locklin. Diaz-Balart won by more than 40 points in 2022. In District 27, Republican incumbent Maria Elvira Salazar leads by four-tenths of a percentage point over her Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez. Salazar won the seat by double digits during the 2022 midterm election. What Happens Next Attention will now turn to 2028, when Florida voters will again weigh in on all of the state’s U.S. House seats, its U.S. Senate seat, and the presidency. The election will offer another test of whether Democrats’ improved margins in 2026 signal a more competitive Florida or whether Republicans can maintain their grip on the state.
news.summary: This year's midterm election results are raising questions about whether the state could become more competitive in 2028.
news.author: Anna Skinner

news.title: Black voters showed up. It’s time to put the ‘couch’ talk to bed.
news.text:
Black voters across the U.S. mobilized in this year’s midterms, proving essential in remaking the electoral map for Democrats.

Black students organized in key states against voter suppression tactics. Black voters collectively endured long lines, overcame a wave of targeted disinformation and, in some cases, defied threats of federal intervention en route to a “Blacklash” that was key to Democrats’ “blue tsunami.” 

Simply put, Black voters turned up and showed out. And with that, it’s past time to retire the tired rhetoric about Black voters prioritizing the couch over voting.

You have likely heard this trope emphasized over the years, in what can feel like an agonizing tradition. We’re sold an image of crucial Black voters loafing around at home, rather than feeling motivated enough to vote. And even when promoted by seemingly well-meaning voices who want more Black folks to vote, the trope is steeped in some pretty harmful stereotypes about Black people — Black men, in particular.

I certainly detected a whiff of this narrative in the coverage of Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s supposed struggles with Black voters and the potential for many of these voters to stay home. Neither came to fruition.

https://twitter.com/CraigDMauger/status/2115802693709295988

And yet, this kind of rhetoric about unmotivated Black voters has become cyclical. Georgia’s Stacey Abrams has gone on the record in dispelling some of these same narratives that swirled around her gubernatorial bid and Kamala Harris’ presidential bid, yet never materialized.

And, to be clear, I understand this as a tactic for voter mobilization groups. Part of me says, “Do what you gotta do to turn out voters.” And in this sense, that means playing on Black people’s desire not to be branded as lazy.

But it’s a misguided obsession — and a particularly irresponsible one for the media to harp on. I’ve never seen any evidence to suggest, for example, that the number of Black people who stand to willfully abstain from voting in any election exceeds the number of Black people who see their right to vote denied or compromised, due to voter suppression tactics. And so it seems reckless to lend more attention to the abstention talk than to address voter suppression — which the news media ought to do more.

Black people have made it abundantly clear that they are not apathetic when it comes to democracy. Frustration over this contrary narrative was the focus of a recent discussion I joined with Black Men Vote, a nonprofit voter mobilization group. As I explained, I’m a relatively young Black man with a pretty comfortable couch, and yet I’ve never felt any urge to choose it over voting. (Sorry, Wayfair.)

And I’m not extraordinary in that regard. The midterms are yet more proof.
news.author: Kaivan Shroff

news.title: US elections: Voters reject Trump and the politics which divided America
news.text:
The incumbent Republican senator for Texas, John Cornyn, for example, fell out of favour with Trump due to a perceived lack of enthusiasm for the latter’s presidential bids and a failure to challenge to the results of the 2020 presidential election. Earlier this year, Trump backed the Texas state attorney Ken Paxton, a polarising figure in Texas who used his role to challenge the 2020 election, as well as abortion laws and DEI legislation.

In Texas, “you have a crappy economy, you have a really bad [Republican] opponent, and a really good [Democrat] candidate”, said Austin native Chris Oakland. “I think when Trump endorsed Paxton, that was when we started to believe that Talarico really was a possibility.

“John Cornyn would have been re-elected, 100%.”

Talarico’s win over Paxton was announced relatively early in the evening, followed a couple of minutes later by the news that stunned the crowd: Democrat Gina Hinojosa had secured the Texas governorship in a fierce race against the long-standing Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.

“For a female Hispanic Democrat to win governor, that’s a lot harder than a white male seminarian in Texas,” said Oakland.

After voting for Trump in the 2024 elections, young men and Latinos in Texas and across the US swung back to the Democrats during the midterms this month. This year, 59% of young men voted for a Democratic US House candidate, according to the AP VoteCast data; compared with 56% of young men who supported Trump in 2024.

At the election watch party in Austin, I spoke with a Texan student called John, a member of a college fraternity with “a wild mix” of Democrats and Republicans.

“I would say among my age group and my cohort of guys, a lot of them saw being a Maga Republican as the masculine thing to do,” he said. “They thought that following Trump and listening to [Maga] and, you know, listening to the super alpha males that are online; they thought it would make them tougher. And they would get more women… I think as we’ve grown up and as we’ve gone through the first couple years of college, a lot of it has changed.

“They’re not as diehard fans of Trump because they see what’s going on, and they see that he might not be as truthful about things as they thought he was in the past.”

Largely ignoring the economy and Iran war, Republicans messaging during the midterms, and particular in Texas, relied heavily on culture war talking points, such as trans people and shariah law, which had previously been effective at rallying conservative voters to the polls. The Republican election post-mortem has already pointed to a failure to talk about the issues that really mattered to American voters this year.

“I would focus not on ballrooms and not renaming things,” said Benjamin Shrader, chairman of the Austin Young Republicans.

Senior Republican figures also engaged in deeply personalised and bigoted attacks on Democrat candidates which alienated swing voters bearing the brunt of rising gas and grocery prices.

Trump called Abdul El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official and the Democrat senate candidate in Michigan, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists”, adding that El-Sayed would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate”.

US vice president JD Vance defended a now notorious ad run by the Republican candidate for Ohio governor Vivek Ramaswamy who was ultimately defeated by Democrat Amy Acton. The ad featured the estranged mother of Acton — who Acton had not spoken to since her mother’s husband was charged with raping Acton as a 12-year-old girl.

In remarks to the media, Vance suggested that Talarico was gay. While during a campaign rally in the conservative Texan ranching town of Weatherford, where souvenir stands sold T-shirts saying ‘Vance-Trump ‘28: Finish the Job’, Vance implied that Democrat senate nominee had an inappropriate focus on trans children.

“I need you to tell James Talarico that his weird obsession with trans kids is not good for the state of Texas,” said Vance to the crowd gathered in Weatherford.

Talarico did not directly respond to Vance but in his victory speech on Tuesday night in Austin he said: “I think it’s safe to say that we are tired of being pitted against each other. We are tired of being told to hate each other. It has been 10 years of this kind of politics. Politics as blood sport. Politics as trolling and owning. Politics as professional wrestling.

“It tears families apart. It ends friendships, and it leaves us all feeling terrible all the time.

“People across the political spectrum are hungry for a different kind of politics. Not a politics of hate. Not a politics of fear. Not a politics of division, but a politics of love.”

Both Talarico and Adam Hamilton, the successful senate candidate in Kansas and a pastor, effectively used faith-based rhetoric in their campaigns that appealed to moderate voters.

During his campaign, Hamilton told CNN: “Scripture says out of the abundance of the mouth, the heart speaks. And so when...when somebody says routinely things that are belittling, demeaning, that says something about what’s going on in their heart.”

While after securing his senate seat, Talarico told a rapt crowd: “My faith teaches me that love is the strongest force in the universe. Love, love is not passive. Love is not neutral. Love is not weak. Love requires that we stand between the bullies and the bullied.”

Talarico and Hamilton represent the next generation of Democrat political talent which has emerged from these midterms — a broad coalition that also includes a slew of elected left-wing Democrats such as El-Sayed.

The end of the midterms marks the kick-off for the 2028 presidential cycle.

Former vice president Kamala Harris is still considered a possible candidate, as well as Alexandria Ocasio Cortez, the 38-year-old congresswoman from New York who has been a strong fundraiser and leading left-wing figure in the Democratic Party.

Democratic presidential contenders now also includes Jon Ossoff, who secured his second term as a senator for Georgia, a purple state that Trump narrowly took in the last election. While, with his eight-year term as governor of California ending in January 2027, Gavin Newsom will have ample time to focus on a presidential bid. Andy Beshear, the popular governor of Kentucky also had a good election as leader of the Democrats Governor Association.

In the Republican field, Vance will face a battle to distance himself from both Trump and the political rhetoric that he engaged in during this election cycle. Among moderate Republicans who rejected Trump in this election cycle, Marco Rubio’s appeal is likely to grow, particularly if the US secretary of state distances himself from Trump and leaves the administration ahead of the 2028 elections.

Ron DeSantis, who launched a presidential bid in 2024, may also emerge as a viable Republican nominee. The Florida governor regularly called out the cost-of-living crisis, as well as the Iran war, before Vance did.

In an interview with Fox News after the elections, DeSantis said: “A lot of our voters who stayed home, they stayed home because they were frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate. That’s just a fact. They were promised big things, and they didn’t deliver it.”
news.summary: The Republican election postmortem has already pointed to a failure to talk about the issues that really mattered to American voters this year, writes Hannah McCarthy from Texas
news.author: Hannah McCarthy,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: From Kenwood to Washington, an inside look at Illinois’ newest senator, Juliana Stratton
news.text:
Senator-elect Juliana Stratton is best known for her work as lieutenant governor, her “F*** Trump” campaign slogan and for being a proud South Sider.

But she’s also a Beyoncé fan and a self-proclaimed “house head,” which was on full display on Election Night as Stratton showed off her dance moves to Cajmere’s 1992 Chicago house classic, “Percolator.”

Here are some things you may not know about Illinois’ newest senator, who alongside Sen. Tammy Duckworth will make Illinois the first state in U.S. history to have two women of color serving simultaneously in the U.S. Senate.

Stratton, 61, has completed five marathons and seven triathlons — and she started training at age 40. She now runs along the Lakefront Trail, bikes to yoga at Millennium Park and goes to Studio Yogi in the South Shore neighborhood. She’s also a meditation fan. 

‘House head’

She is a “house head” and left a campaign event in late October to head to a house dance party. Stratton says she wants to host a house dance party in Washington for other “house head” colleagues in Congress. Stratton goes to house music parties at Visions Odeum and Events in West Pullman.

Stratton is a “major” Beyoncé fan and has a placard on her desk that reads “What would Beyoncé do?” She was also in the audience for an Oprah Winfrey show that featured Beyoncé, and was so lively that the show’s producers asked her to come back to be part of the audience.

Prior to her run for state representative in 2016, Stratton was a mediator at an alternative dispute resolution firm for 20 years. One of her cases was between a teenager who vandalized a store and the store owner. Instead of pressing charges, she helped to broker a deal to help the teen work in the store to pay back damages.

Stratton graduated from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign in 1987 with a bachelor’s degree in broadcast journalism. Stratton grew up in the Pill Hill neighborhood and went to Kenwood Academy High School. Her first elected office was parent representative and later chair of the Kenwood Academy Local School Council.

Stratton is a member of the Alpha Kappa Alpha Sorority, the country’s first intercollegiate Black sorority, which was founded in 1908 at Howard University. It’s part of a group of historically Black sororities and fraternities commonly known as the “Divine Nine.” AKA now has more than 1,000 chapters and over 300,000 initiated members worldwide. The organization’s headquarters is on the South Side of Chicago at 5656 Stony Island Ave. Former Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Rep. Lauren Underwood are also members of the sorority.

South Side bites

Stratton lives in Bronzeville and frequents South Side restaurants and bakeries like Virtue in Hyde Park, Brown Sugar Bakery in Greater Grand Crossing neighborhood, Ain’t She Sweet Cafe in Bronzeville and Strugglebeard in Hyde Park. She’s not a coffee drinker but loves a London Fog.

Family history

Stratton’s great-great grandfather was enslaved and freed by the Emancipation Proclamation. He helped to co-found the town of Stevensville, Mississippi — which was his last name.
news.author: Tina Sfondeles

news.title: Keir Starmer cashes in on lucrative speaking gigs after quitting No10 as he signs up with US-based agency which boasts Joe Biden, Jacinda Ardern and Kamala Harris among its clients
news.text:
Sir Keir Starmer is set to cash in on lucrative speaking gigs after being turfed out of Downing Street by signing up with a US-based agency.

The former prime minister, who was ousted by Andy Burnham in July, has taken up a paid role with Creative Artists Agency (CAA).

The Los Angeles-headquartered firm also boasts former US president Joe Biden and Jacinda Ardern, the former prime minister of New Zealand, on its books.

Other clients include failed US presidential candidate Kamala Harris, human rights lawyer Amal Clooney and actress Gwyneth Paltrow.

It is the first paid employment that Sir Keir has found since he quit Westminster entirely by resigning as MP for Holborn and St Pancras in September.

The 64-year-old sought advice from Sir Laurie Magnus, the independent adviser on ministerial standards, on taking up the role.

A profile on the CAA website states that Sir Keir 'offers a rare insider's perspective on the geopolitical, economic, and security forces reshaping Europe and the wider world'.

It adds that he 'brings firsthand insight into leading through uncertainty, driving change, and delivering results under immense pressure'.

The profile continues: 'For business and financial audiences, he connects geopolitical decisions directly to markets, investment, competitiveness, private capital, and the global business environment.

'From Ukraine and European security to shifting alliances and political instability, Sir Keir helps audiences understand what today's global upheaval could mean for governments, businesses, and society.'

The profile boasts of Sir Keir's work as a barrister, his role as director of public prosecutions in England and Wales, and his achievements in taking Labour from opposition and into government.

But it doesn't mention how his two-year premiership saw him lose the faith of Labour MPs and succumb to a coup by Mr Burnham and his allies.

Whitehall's business appointment rules require all former ministers to seek the advice of Sir Laurie for all work they wish to take up for a period of two years after leaving office.

In his advice to Sir Keir, Sir Laurie reminded the ex-premier he should not draw on any privileged information available to him when he was PM in his new role.

Sir Keir was also told not to become personally involved in lobbying the Government on behalf of CAA for a two-year period.

It comes after Rachel Reeves, who served as Sir Keir's chancellor, also signed up with corporate speaking agencies.

She sought approval to go on the books of the Washington Speakers Bureau and Chartwell Speakers Bureau.

Her profile on the Chartwell Speakers website describes her as 'one of the UK's most prominent economic and political figures'.
news.summary: The former prime minister, who was ousted by Andy Burnham in July, has taken up a paid role with Creative Artists Agency (CAA).
news.author: Editor,Greg Heffer

news.title: On the Ground in the Final Days Before Trump’s Midterm Debacle
news.text:
Jacob Hawk leaned over the plastic fencing to get Vivek Ramaswamy’s attention as the Republican candidate for Ohio governor moved down the line shaking hands at the Ohio University branch campus in Chillicothe, six days before the midterm elections. Hawk held onto Ramaswamy’s hand and started trying to tell him everything he was dealing with, everything he wanted the Republican candidates gathered there to help him with.

Hawk, 39, told him that he was a self-employed landscaper who was having a hard time with the high cost of fuel. He told him that he was raising three young kids from two different moms, mostly on his own. He told him of his worries for his 9-year-old son, who was autistic and underweight and suffered from a two-year delay in brain development.

Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, nodded and offered some token reassurance and moved down the line, toward the arena where he would soon be appearing with President Donald Trump and Sen. Jon Husted and the rest of the Republican slate in a state that Trump had won by 11 percentage points two years ago, and which the party had dominated during the era of Trump. I had been at many Republican events in the state over that time, including a rally in an airplane hangar outside Dayton in March 2016, where a giant crowd had roared as Trump’s jet had rolled into view and where he had declared that he had come to save Ohio. “Our jobs are being sucked away,” he said then. “It’s unbelievable what’s happening.”

This event was different. Ten years had passed, and gone was the fierce bravado of Trump the conquering hero, bristling with retribution and promises. This rally was populated largely by the same sort of voters who had been particularly drawn to Trump all along, working-class Midwesterners who had not been engaged in politics before he came on the scene. But there were fewer of them — the campaign had chosen an arena that held only 2,000 — and their devotion had been subsumed by uncertainty. They were still with Trump, but they weren’t sure how to reconcile their own difficulties with the fact that he was the president during this trying time.

Take gas prices, which “are beating the hell out of me,” Hawk told me. He was trying his best not to hold them against Trump and his decision to go to war against Iran, instead faulting Congress for limiting domestic oil drilling. “The president has to go find oil in another country because Congress won’t let him find it in our country,” he said, overlooking the fact that Trump’s party has controlled both houses of Congress during his second term.

Nearby, Debbie Shock, a 57-year-old mail carrier, blamed the high fuel costs on “the stock exchange, the markets — they’re the ones that control it.” “We have oil right here in the U.S.,” she said. “Why are we buying it from other countries to begin with?”

Shock fit a profile I had gotten to know well in 2016: an Obama-Trump voter. She was loyal to Trump — “I like the man. Nobody’s perfect, you know what I mean?” — and told me she would never go back to Democrats now. Why not? I asked. “They’re covering up the child molestation,” she said. What did she mean by that? “I’ve heard stories about the sex trafficking. The Clintons are involved in it, Disney World, you know, all that.”

It would be easy to ridicule such murky talk, yet it was not much less coherent than what soon emerged on the arena stage, which was streamed on a large screen for the few hundred of us who were out on the lawn outside the arena. Trump has never been known for structured oratory, but it is hard to overstate the extent to which his digressive style has advanced since 2016, and to convey how surreal it is to experience firsthand, as the reality of what presidential communication has come to in 2026.

The rally opened with the customary introductory video of late-era Trump, an explicitly messianic framing: “God said, ‘I need someone who will be strong and courageous,’” the voice-over intones. “So God made Trump.”

Thus introduced, Trump opened his remarks with a lengthy disquisition on Husted’s body, which had newly become part of his routine. “I looked at Jon and studied his physique,” he cooed, after referring to his recent comments on Husted’s “ass.” “I studied the feet, the legs, the shoulders. I tapped him on the shoulder, and it was like hitting a piece of steel.”

When a protester inside the arena started shouting something — those of us outside couldn’t hear what — and was removed, Trump bid him good riddance: “Now he goes home and his boyfriend gets upset with him.”

There were protesters outside, too, and things were starting to heat up between them and the supporters. “What are you talking about, ‘boyfriend?’” shouted one protester, a young man. “He was just talking about Jon Husted’s ass! That’s not gay??”

A supporter in front of me, a bearded man in his 50s, stewed as he watched the protesters. “You’re going to see someone dropping like a bad habit,” he growled, as he started to move toward them, before being held back by the woman who was with him.

A moment later, Trump had moved on to Jeffrey Epstein, saying that the Democrats had protected him for years. “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago,” he declared. “I was the one who was totally exonerated from him. But they use it, because that’s what they do. They’re sick, weak people.”

This set off a new round of shouting outside, as cries of “pedophiles!” flew back and forth.

Suddenly, one Trump supporter near me rushed hard at a protester and knocked him to the ground, his head landing with such a thud on the blacktop that I initially thought it might be a suppressed gunshot. Dozens of officers swarmed to the spot. Cameras flashed.

A few moments later, a couple other protesters, also young men, began railing against the war against Iran. “We’re going to be the ones sent off to die for Israel,” one shouted. “‘America First,’ and you want me to die in the Middle East?”

Trump touched on the war — “they’re getting beaten very badly” — but spent far more time on his home renovations. “The White House has to be beautiful outside, it needs that exterior plaster. The bricks were falling, the stone was broken, the monuments were coming off, the beautiful windows were cracked, it looked terrible, and I fixed it very inexpensively, and now it’s more beautiful than ever,” he said. “And President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness, who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalks, who doesn’t understand that having asphalt going to your main entrance is not the right thing, we’d like to have granite and marble we’d like to have it look nice, you don’t use asphalt, you use asphalt for your streets. …”

On the ramble went. To the Haitians in nearby Springfield: “The town went from no crime to high crime,” but “they’re being moved out.” To a riff on Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s mother calling her a liar, in apparent reference to Acton’s having accused her stepfather of raping her when she was 12, as he was subsequently charged with doing. The ad had met with widespread opprobrium, but Trump defended Ramaswamy. “The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar, that she is no good. … How the hell is that his problem?” To “O Canada, which has been ripping us off for years,” and Somalia, “which isn’t even a country,” and “transgender mutilization,” and his plan to rename the Strait of Hormuz for himself.

Finally, Trump ceded the stage to Husted and Ramaswamy. But by then, the lawn had emptied out as people drifted home, Jacob Hawk among them. A vendor was shouting out discount prices on his MAGA merchandise. “$10 special on hats! All the hats are $10! These are normally $25 hats. That’s a good hat for $10.”

The next day, the full Republican slate of statewide candidates appeared, sans Trump, at a small pep rally inside a former Delphi auto-parts factory in Vandalia, outside Dayton. It is an enormous building that employed more than 100 prior to its closing in 2009 and is now being used as a warehouse by a company that sells air conditioners, employing only 10 or so; Delphi announcements still remained on the bulletin boards, adding a ghostly feel.

The setting was an unintentional reminder of what Ohio has been through. Between 2000 and 2025, the state lost 300,000 manufacturing jobs, a devastation that had made it highly susceptible to Trump’s message in 2016. But Republicans have been in charge of the state since 2010, and so it was the task of the candidates gathered there, with an audience of just a few dozen, to cast the state as being on an upswing. Complicating this challenge is the fact that so much of the state’s recent growth has been concentrated in the Columbus area: countless data centers, defense contractor Anduril, a massive Intel plant under construction.

The bigger challenge, though, was the nationwide pall that hung over the event: the reality of stubbornly high inflation and high gas prices, the latter a direct consequence of Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. He had stood against costly foreign entanglements when he ran in 2016, in opposition to his party’s recent record, and carried that same banner again in 2024. But another aspect of his political persona had prevailed: a heedless swagger that, in this case, had been fanned by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. It had led him into this drawn-out conflict that has already cost U.S. taxpayers more than $47 billion.

And it had left a long row of Republican candidates standing in this giant building stacked high with made-in-China air conditioners all but pleading the small assemblage to save them from the political climate. “You can’t give up,” Husted said. “This is a Republican state, and the only way Democrats can win is if Republicans don’t vote.” 

Five days later, I was in York County, Pennsylvania, which Trump had won by 25 points in 2024, and which was home to one of four Republican-held House districts targeted by Democrats. I chose to go to a precinct on the outskirts of York, thinking it would offer a diverse cross-section, in between more Democratic York proper and more Republican rural areas. But over 90 minutes of conversations, I didn’t encounter a Republican voter until I was about to call it a day.

The first person I spoke with, Bill, a 52-year-old state government employee who asked that I not use his last name for fear of losing his job, had voted for Trump three times. He hardly considered himself MAGA but was drawn in 2016 to Trump’s “drain the swamp” rhetoric and his disavowal of the war in Iraq. He voted for him again in 2020 and 2024 because he didn’t think much of Joe Biden and Kamala Harris.

But on this day, Bill was coming to vote against his Republican representative, Scott Perry, because he was too “Trump adjacent.” Bill had finally had enough of Trump, especially when it came to all the revelations of self-dealing involving his family and cronies. “I will not be falling for him again,” he told me. “Drain the swamp, no wars. … It was all a lie.”

He said he couldn’t understand how Trump had gone from America First to seemingly letting the country’s foreign policy be dictated by Israel. He said that he was voting for the Democrats mainly just for the sake of “gridlock,” as deliberate blockage. “Someone’s got to stop this,” he said. “It’s getting out of control.”

Each Democratic voter I spoke with after that was coming with their own motivation for voting against the Republican slate, like the cast of “Murder on the Orient Express.”

For Annie (who also asked that I not use her last name), it was for Trump’s social-welfare cuts, which had cost her and her disabled husband $300 per month in SNAP benefits and nearly cost them their Medicaid coverage.

For Desiree Edmonds, an elementary school teacher, it was high inflation, which was translating into anxiety among the working-class children in her classroom.

For Mark Castillo, a 19-year-old ironworker, it was for the sky-high cost of diesel.

For Jacqueline Jimenez, a native Puerto Rican who worked as a home-health aide, it was for the excessive harshness of ICE arrests.

For Shiri Kramer, a warehouse worker, it was for the general meanness emanating from the administration, which made her think of her grandfather, a Jewish American who had extended mercy to German POWs during World War II. “My grandfather would be writhing right now,” she said. “Nothing happening in our country is OK.” 

By night’s end, Republicans had lost this Pennsylvania district by 10 points, as well as the other three in the state and more than 40 nationwide. They had lost at least seven Senate seats, even in states where Democrats hadn’t prevailed in decades — Kansas, Texas, South Carolina. Incredibly, even Mississippi was on the verge. In Ohio, Republicans lost the race for Senate and governor — only one of the seven statewide candidates on stage at the warehouse emerged a victor — as well as two Republican-held House seats, a stark reversal in a state that had seemed to be trending away from Democrats for good. In all, Democrats flipped five governorships and up to 12 state legislative chambers. The Democratic popular-vote margin in congressional races nationwide was 13 percentage points — nearly double the Republican margin in their own wave years of 2010 and 1994, and approaching the scale of the historic Democratic rout in the post-Watergate election of 1974.

The particularly stunning loss of the South Carolina seat brought to mind a warning issued in May 2016 by Lindsey Graham, whose death this July left the seat vacant. “If we nominate Trump, we will get destroyed…….and we will deserve it,” Graham tweeted in 2016. For years, the Republican Party had avoided the catastrophic reckoning he warned of — through Trump’s narrow win in 2016, through the Jan. 6, 2021, assault on the Capitol, through Biden’s fateful insistence on running for reelection at age 81 in 2024. Along the way, much of the party, including Graham himself, had accommodated itself to Trump. One way of looking at the 2026 results was that the warning had finally come true. The reckoning had been delayed by a decade, but it had gathered more force over time, like a boulder rolling downhill.

There was a hint of such a reckoning in the words that Bill, the three-time Trump voter, left me with in York. After he returned from voting, he bade me farewell with a parting regret.

“You see what’s going on,” he said, “and you’re like, ‘What the hell did I do?’”
news.author: Alec Macgillis

news.title: Democrats, Republicans Asking For Money As Vote Counting Persists Days Later
news.text:
As two Senate seats remain uncalled, the campaign arms for the Republican and Democratic parties are calling on donors to chip in more funds for their candidates to cross the finish line — despite all votes already being cast.

Days after polls closed, the vote count is still ongoing for Senate seats in Alaska and Mississippi. The National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC) and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) have created recount funds to finance the drawn-out fights, Politico reported Thursday.

As of Friday a pair of the Senate races on opposite sides of the country remain too close to call. Democratic Mississippi senate nominee Scott Colom held a razor-thin 2,000-vote lead at 49.1 percent of the vote with incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith close behind at 48.8 percent, the Associated Press reported early Friday afternoon. More than 95 percent of the race’s ballots were counted at the time.

Meanwhile in the Last Frontier, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola was ahead holding 48.17 percent of the vote, while Republican Alaska Sen. Dan Sullivan trailed at 47.8 percent after 74% of ballots were counted, according to the outlet. Unlike Mississippi, Alaska uses ranked-choice voting (RCV) to tabulate its results if no candidate receives a majority of the vote. (RELATED: ‘Decoy’ Senate Candidate Under Investigation Over Alleged Voter Confusion Scheme)

Before polls closed in Alaska on Election Day, the NRSC established the “NRSC RECOUNT FUND,” signing on Sullivan’s campaign, Politico reported. The NRSC then brought in Cindy Hyde-Smith’s campaign the following day.

The DSCC has also followed suit and is seeking action from supporters for the long haul.

Former vice president and failed 2024 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris rallied supporters on her email list, calling for increased attention and funding to the Mississippi race, Politico reported.

“I have spent a lot of time in the South this year, including campaigning with Scott, and I know that our movement has the power to do it,: Harris wrote in the email. “Republicans are going to do everything they can to try and hold onto this seat. They’ve taken so many losses that they will not let another go without a fight.”

The DSCC did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

The NRSC announced they would send a letter to County Election Commissioners and Circuit Clerks in Mississippi, demanding they separate and preserve all affidavit ballots cast in the Nov. 3, 2026 general election, the NRSC said in a Thursday press release sent to the DCNF.

“As the democratic process continues to play out, we are committed to ensuring that every single lawful ballot is accurately counted and the voices of all Mississippians are heard,” NRSC Regional Press Secretary Samantha Cantrell said in the release.

The Senate GOP’s campaign arm expects results to be finally tabulated in Mississippi by next week, but results for Alaska could take until November 18. 

A spokesperson from the NRSC referred the DCNF to two memos from the Alaskan incumbent’s campaign office. 

“If the ranked choice voting tabulation took place today of the votes that we have in hand right now, Senator Dan Sullivan would defeat Mary Peltola 105,037 to 104,709, a margin of 328 vote,” a memo from Sullivan’s office released Wednesday said.

“The Division of Elections has ~20,000 early votes and ~27,000 absentee ballots in hand that we believe will not be counted until Nov. 10, with late mail and questioned ballots still to come,” a new memo released Friday said. “Sullivan needs about 49.5% of the two-way vote in what is left. He has 49.8% of the two-way vote counted so far.”

The Senate race in Alaska has drawn much scrutiny during the midterm cycle, after a political unknown sharing the same name as the Republican incumbent threw his hat in the race, causing the Department of Justice (DOJ) to sue the state, alleging intentional voter confusion at the polls.

Though the pending lawsuit was thrown out by a federal judge, the DOJ said it plans to re-file for litigation.

Should neither Sullivan nor Peltola clear 50 percent in the first round, RCV tabulation is expected in mid-November, Politico reported.

Senate campaigns raised at least $1.3 billion for this year’s midterms, according to data from the Federal Election Commission (FEC).
news.summary: ‘democratic process continues to play out’
news.author: Libby Bandelin

news.title: Is There a Left Candidate for President?
news.text:
The race for 2028 is already starting, and progressives are all asking one question: Who will take up the left’s mantle in the next presidential election? 

An obvious first choice for many self-described leftists, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., has said she is seriously considering a run. Ocasio-Cortez laid the groundwork for a potential presidential bid rooted in economic populism and “fighting oligarchy” while campaigning alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., for midterm candidates around the country this cycle. 

Democratic strategists, however, have pointed out it would be far easier for Ocasio-Cortez to run for Democratic New York Sen. Chuck Schumer’s seat in 2028; and it’s even possible the 75-year-old presumptive majority leader will retire.

There isn’t a clear pick for another Democratic candidate with star power who could mount a truly progressive campaign — presenting the left with the threat of losing the momentum that fueled a democratic socialist wave during the primaries and animated campaigns across the ideological spectrum on Tuesday. 

That, said her former spokesperson Lauren Hitt, is not Ocasio-Cortez’s problem.

“I think the wrong reason to run would be because nobody else is running in the progressive lane,” said Hitt, who now advises progressive and moderate candidates. “She has made a lot of good investments in the midterms and in helping build up the progressive bench, but it was not her job to make sure we had another person to run.”

(Representatives for Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

So if Ocasio-Cortez doesn’t run from the left, who will?

The Field So Far

Candidates exploring potential presidential bids include a few newer faces alongside a very similar cast of moderates who campaigned for the Democratic nomination in the 2016 and 2020 primaries.

Names like New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, and even the party’s former nominee Kamala Harris are making the rounds; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., has also laid the groundwork for a run. The recently reelected Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has long been viewed as a potential contender, as has Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, though he said last month he’s not planning on a run.

None of them are people you would necessarily liken to someone like Ocasio-Cortez or the grandfather of the movement behind her, Sanders himself.

Rep. Ro Khanna of California is so far the most “progressive” person openly considering a run. Khanna served as national co-chair of Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, and he’s long been a voice for an anti-interventionist foreign policy. He drew the ire of tech billionaires for supporting a wealth tax in California. 

Yet there’s a palpable skepticism around Khanna among leftists, even if they can’t quite put their finger on why. Some weren’t impressed when he defended his support for funding Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense system after publicizing an arrest in the West Bank earlier this year. (Khanna later came out against funding the Iron Dome). And as a multimillionaire, he’s also drawn criticism from the right and the left for his personal wealth.

Like Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna has said he will back Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., for House Speaker despite pledges from other candidates to withhold their support for either Jeffries or Schumer, both moderates, for leadership positions next session. 

Leveraging Economic Populism

It’s still incredibly early, but there’s one unifying theme emerging from Tuesday’s results for whichever candidate decides to try to court the progressive vote.

“All I know is that the populist lane is wide open for someone to seize it,” said Ravi Mangla, the spokesperson for the Working Families Party. 

Victories over the past two years, from Zohran Mamdani’s election as mayor of New York City to the clutch of democratic socialists and progressives heading to Congress in January, show that Democrats can marshal discontent with Donald Trump and the far right to elect candidates running on progressive policies.

”Voters were very clear: People are very, very angry,” said Greg Krieg, a progressive Democratic strategist who works with Slingshot Strategies and is the spokesperson for the pro-Palestine super PAC American Priorities. “There is a focus on economic populism that transcends the ideological splits in the party.”

With the rising cost of living, and candidates tapping into that populism, the question for progressives is how to best wield the blue version of economic populism against the right-wing version that powered Trump’s rise. 

“Right-wing populism didn’t really defeat left-wing populism, it just ran against a kind of corporate slop for many years,” Krieg said. 

This era’s new “kitchen table” issues are a constellation of economic woes that voters are increasingly connecting to the forces concentrating wealth and political power in the hands of the few. Democrats should respond to that by fighting, visibly, against the things that take money out of people’s pockets, corruption and price-gouging among them, Krieg said. 

“I think that the American people, if they are presented a choice of right-wing populism and left-wing populism, will opt for the left-wing populism,” Krieg said. “And I think that’s quadruply true now that we’ve done the right-wing populism experiment and it’s been such a fiasco — so let’s give them that option.” 

The factors influencing how Democrats approach 2028 are taking shape now. They include the debate over who will lead the party in the House and Senate, though any effort to stop Schumer or Jeffries from leading roles would face long odds. And how Democrats fare in the next presidential race will depend in large part on what they do with their control of Congress during the last two years of Trump’s final term in office.

DSA Endorsement?

Then there is the group that helped power the rise of Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani, the next mayors of Washington and Los Angeles, and the largest incoming bloc of socialist members of Congress in history: the Democratic Socialists of America.

Any candidate that gets buy-in from DSA will have to support policies like Medicare for All, taxing the rich, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on U.S. arms to Israel. DSA, which endorsed both Sanders’s 2016 and 2020 primary bids, is running a presidential exploratory committee that will eventually vote to endorse a candidate after collecting input from its members. 

DSA passed a resolution to explore a 2028 endorsement at its national convention last year. And there isn’t necessarily a consensus among its members — more than 125,000 people across 130 chapters in 43 states — on whether or not they want to see Ocasio-Cortez run, said Ella Teevan, who chairs the group’s presidential exploratory group and sits on its National Political Committee.

“The Bernie case feels just a little bit different because I think the membership was a little bit more united around Bernie, although by no means unanimously,” Teevan said. “If and when we do consider an AOC endorsement, hers will be a little bit more contentious. But like I said, that’s the beauty of DSA.”

Though Ocasio-Cortez is no shoo-in, DSA members haven’t coalesced around any other candidate — and it’s not clear they will. 

“I know that there are other quote-unquote progressives who might be considering a presidential run in 2028, but I think it’s really clear for us that they need to support DSA’s core demands that most people in the United States support,” Teevan said. 

“If a candidate were to come along who supported those policies, I think a considerable portion of membership would think about whether we should endorse them,” she said. “But yeah, I don’t think that there’s a natural other person with name recognition in the field that, at least, I can think of right now.”

And there may yet be candidates who enter the race who aren’t yet on the radar, said Hitt, Ocasio-Cortez’s former spokesperson: “It’s totally possible there’s a progressive champion who could fill that lane that we aren’t even thinking of yet.”

news.title: Humiliated Trump Rushes to MAGA-Fied Network for First Interview Since Election Disaster
news.text:
The president is scrambling to a network owned by a Trump-friendly billionaire for his first in-depth interview since Republicans suffered sweeping losses in the midterms.

Trump is slated to tape an interview Friday for Sunday’s 60 Minutes, CNN’s Brian Stelter reported on X. The sit-down is Trump’s first in-depth interview since the Republican Party’s midterm losses on Tuesday, and CBS News sources confirmed the plan to CNN while cautioning it hasn’t taken place yet. 

The White House schedule lists “a pre-tape interview” at 10:30 a.m. Eastern. It is a high-profile stage, since 60 Minutes is the highest-rated newsmagazine on American TV.

The interviewer is Ross Douthat, a conservative former New York Times columnist who joined 60 Minutes as a correspondent and has frequently been critical of Trump. He previously interviewed Vice President JD Vance for his Times podcast. In a column earlier this week, Douthat depicted the midterms as a failure of “the New Right.”

The day after the midterms, Trump spoke to reporters at the site of his $600 million White House ballroom project without mentioning the election results once. 

CBS News reported Thursday that Trump will use his lame-duck period to prioritize building his presidential library in Miami. “The president’s attention is all over the place,” a former White House official who remains close to the administration told MS NOW. “How many people are preparing briefs on what marble to pick for X project?”

One longtime Trump adviser said the 80-year-old president is not as upset about the midterms as people might expect, since he can return to “his happy place” of overseeing renovation and real estate projects. “His skyscraper just got cut down by 30 percent, and he is gonna find a way to rebuild,” the adviser said.

Trump last appeared on 60 Minutes in April, in an interview with Norah O’Donnell that turned contentious. He called her a “disgrace” and said, “You’re horrible people.”

He refused a traditional pre-election 60 Minutes interview in 2024. His opponent, Kamala Harris, sat for one, and Trump then sued CBS, claiming it was deceptively edited. Legal experts said the suit was frivolous, but CBS’ owners at the time paid Trump $16 million to make the matter go away, sparking outrage across the news industry.

Trump-friendly billionaire David Ellison acquired CBS’ parent company Paramount last August and installed Bari Weiss, pro-Trump cofounder of the conservative outlet The Free Press, as its head of news. Under Weiss, the network saw upheaval and internal tension that led to the exits of several of its biggest anchor stars, much of it stemming from her changes to 60 Minutes.

Weiss also shelved a segment critical of the Trump administration’s decision to deport migrants to a notorious prison in El Salvador, part of her efforts to overhaul the show.

Producers at the show are questioning whether it is worth pursuing “politically sensitive” stories if Weiss will not “stand behind them when the Trump administration inevitably lashes out.” 

“Why take the risk of pursuing a tough story, the thinking goes, if the people at the top might throw you overboard at the first sign of political blowback?” wrote Status’ Oliver Darcy.

The White House has been contacted for comment.
