news.title: D.C. Memo: The midterms were all about enthusiasm
news.text:
WASHINGTON – As analysts pore over the results of the midterm election, one thing that has become apparent is that increased enthusiasm of the voters propelled the Democratic wave that swept the country. 

There is also evidence of a dampening of Republican enthusiasm for GOP candidates this year.

That can be most clearly seen in the 1st Congressional District race, where Rep. Brad Finstad is trailing Democratic challenger Jake Johnson by 323 votes with the results likely headed for a recount.

In unofficial results, Finstad received 162,733 votes while Johnson received 163,056.

In 2024, when President Donald Trump was at the top of the GOP ticket, Finstad won 220,929 votes while his Republican challenger, Rachel Bohman, won 156,375. Finstad even outperformed Trump in the 1st District in that election. 

So, there was an increase of votes for a Democrat in this midterm and a huge drop in the votes for Finstad from two years ago.

Trump urged voters to cast their ballots in the midterm as if he was on the ballot. 

And in a way, he was. But not in a good way for the GOP as the giant blue wave that washed over the nation Tuesday was considered a referendum on Trump’s presidency and a reason GOP voters were not enthusiastic to show up at the polls. It also served to turn out Democrats and independents who voted for Democrats. 

“Trump has delivered a steady diet of disruption in his second term,” said Carleton College political science professor emeritus Steven Schier. “ICE controversies, high gas prices, a war without an apparent end in sight, tariffs that roil rural producers. He made the election about himself and, with the diet he has provided, received repudiation nationally and in Minnesota.”

Schier said that in Minnesota, the election centered on Trump, not fraud, even as Republican candidates fervently and continuously attacked Democrats on the issues.

There were decisive victories of Democrats in all statewide offices.

“It’s far from clear that the GOP will ever be competitive in statewide elections again,” Schier said. “Minnesota seems to be going the way of Oregon and Washington. All are states with large populations of highly educated white voters who have turned away from Trump this year.”

Outperforming Harris in Greater Minnesota

Greater enthusiasm for a Democratic candidate can also be determined from Tuesday’s results in the 2nd Congressional District.

Retiring Rep. Angie Craig, who represents the district now, won 165,183 votes in the last midterm, held in 2022. Craig’s Democratic rival, Joe Teirab, won 148, 576 votes.

In this midterm, 214,255 ballots were cast for Democratic Rep.-elect Matt Little and 160,636 were cast for his rival, state Sen. Eric Pratt.

So, more votes were cast in that district for its representative to Congress than were cast two years ago, with many more of those additional votes going to a Democrat.

In fact, Minnesota broke records for voter turnout in a midterm, with Minnesotans casting about 2.9 million votes. That’s about 11% more ballots than were cast in 2022.

Little said the reason for greater enthusiasm in the 2nd District was the strength of his campaign. “I think our campaign was successful because I said what I believe and people appreciated that,” Little said.

But he also said his decisive victory – he won with 57.1% to 42.8% for Pratt – was also due to voter anger over President Donald Trump and his policies.

That anger drove voters to the Democratic Party across the nation in suburbs and exurbs, which make up much of the area of the 2nd District.

Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan and Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar received fewer votes than the Kamala Harris-Tim Walz ticket did in 2024.

Flanagan received about 1.52 million votes and Klobuchar received about 1.57 million. Meanwhile, the Harris-Walz ticket won nearly 1.66 million votes.

But an analysis by the Flanagan campaign says the Democrat outperformed that Harris-Walz ticket in some parts of the state.

According to that analysis, Flanagan’s biggest gains were in Greater Minnesota, regional centers and suburbs.

It showed an 11.5% shift toward Flanagan in Clay County, a 10.5% shift in Mower County, a 22% shift in St. Louis County and a 19% shift in Olmsted County. Flanagan’s campaign said she did better than Harris in other Greater Minnesota counties as well.

The analysis showed there was a flip from Trump to Flanagan in Winona, Anoka and Blue Earth counties.

Emmer faces another election

The dust has yet to clear from this week’s Republican massacre and the GOP is heading toward another election next week – and Rep. Tom Emmer, R-6th District, who won his race for reelection, could lose this one.

On Tuesday, U.S. House Republicans will hold elections on who will lead them in the new Congress, where they will now be in the minority.

What will be the size of that minority? That’s not determined yet as races across the country are too close to call and some are heading to recounts, like the contest between Rep. Brad Finstad, R-1st District, and Democrat Jake Johnson.

Currently, Democrats have an estimated 50-seat majority over Republicans in the House.

The heavy GOP losses forced House Speaker Mike Johnson to announce he would not seek another leadership position.

In the minority, House Republicans will have only four main leadership posts: minority leader, whip, conference chair and policy committee chair.

Emmer, who is now House majority whip, said he would like to continue to be GOP whip in the minority. But the size of the Republican defeat may have dimmed his chances.

And Texas Rep. August Pfluger is challenging Emmer for that job, which will be the No. 2 Republican leadership position in the next Congress.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., and House Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, are the two announced candidates in the race.

Over in the U.S. Senate, current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said he wants to become Senate Minority Leader but could be challenged for that position.

ICYMI (election edition):

▪️State Government reporter Matt Blake wrote that Minnesota will have another Democratic trifecta, but with Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar at the helm it likely will be different from the one in 2023. (Read Matt’s story on Klobuchar’s victory here).

 ▪️Yes, Minnesota’s Democrats are now in the majority in Congress, but the state will lose a lot of clout as it sends two freshmen to the U.S. Senate, where seniority is the coin of the realm. (Read our story on Peggy Flanagan’s election to the Senate here).

▪️Brian Arola reported on the Jake Johnson campaign and how the Democrat was able to best incumbent Rep. Brad Finstad by fewer than 350 votes in the 1st District race, which is likely headed for a recount. (Here’s Brian’s election-night story).

▪️We also covered Democrat Matt Little’s win in the 1st Congressional District, where he beat state Rep. Eric Pratt. That seat opened up when Angie Craig decided to run for the U.S. Senate.

Please keep your comments, and any questions, coming. I’ll try my best to respond. I can be reached at aradelat@minnpost.com.

news.title: Did Anyone Really Win the Midterms?
news.text:
There wasn't much ambiguity in the results of the 2026 midterm elections. Republicans — all of them, including squishes, establishmentarians, MAGA warriors, and everyone in between — got a good old-fashioned political spanking. 

Who won? Democrats won something: the right to govern a presently ungovernable country and start working on turning their crazy agenda into the law of the land.

They'll be unsuccessful largely because Donald Trump still has a veto pen and the courts, especially the Supreme Court, that haven't yet lost their marbles.

The only true winner of the 2026 midterm elections was Big Government. No one was elected saying they were going to cut the $2 trillion deficit, make our $40 trillion debt more manageable, or find a way to amend Social Security, Medicare, and other entitlements.

"The Democrats don't have a unified agenda, and neither do the Republicans who managed to stay in office," writes Reason.com's Nick Gillespie. "But one thing is clear: Nobody in politics is even gesturing toward cutting the overall size, spending, and scope of government."

Every year, the budget grows larger. Every year, hundreds of new regulations are written, each carrying with them the full force of law, and bureaucrats salivating to enforce them.

Every year, federal agencies get larger; their budgets increase; in many cases, they hire more employees. And agency managers have to work overtime to come up with ways and means to justify their budgets. God forbid they ever take steps to reduce them.

"The only thing we can bet on for sure is that the federal government will almost spend more money next year than this year," writes Gillespie.

It's almost as if both parties have given up trying to manage a government that is out of control. The $7.2 trillion budget is impossible to get your mind around. Understanding how the tens of thousands of individual line items in the budget impact the overall economy, or which ones are necessary and which are unnecessary, is not within the ken of human understanding.

Elections do little more than rearrange the deck chairs on the Titanic. A Harvard study from 2024 pointed out the obvious.

Despite the vast differences in their policy prescriptions, both Democrats and Republicans, as well as Vice President Kamala Harris and former President Donald Trump, are proposing agendas that give the federal government a more muscular and far-reaching role than seen in the recent past. They differ in how and in what areas of personal and commercial life the state will flex its power.

Throw into the mix the present incendiary nature of the politics of extremism and polarization that afflicts Congress, and the ungovernable nature of the United States can't be hidden.

In fact, 89% of company executives call polarization and extremism a threat to the business climate, according to a study by the Conference Board. It is increasingly difficult for executives to stay above the political fray at a time when both employees and consumers are calling on companies to take a stand on social issues such as racism and climate change. Some companies already have scaled back their DEI efforts in response to political pressures, and 68% of executives in the Conference Board survey said they feared retribution from federal elected officials in the next three to five years.

Do you think that people can be considered free if they fear the government? 

We're on the cusp of some kind of collapse. Social, financial, spiritual — perhaps all three. Anyone can see the path we're on is not sustainable. And as long as we insist on fighting over internet memes and other meaningless screaming, our America is under threat.

news.title: Why G2 Esports Ended Its Collaboration With Head Coach Perkz Following His Post on Abortion and Politics
news.text: G2 Esports terminated its collaboration with head coach Luka 'Perkz' Perković after his 4 November 2026 post on X about abortion and politics, citing remarks that conflicted with its values.The retired League of Legends player had written the statement to explain his beliefs and address associations with other public figures. He discussed his Catholic faith, political preferences and relationship with former G2 chief executive Carlos 'ocelote' Rodríguez Santiago.His opposition to abortion drew criticism from fans and fellow players. G2's response referred to several statements, without identifying a single remark as the reason for its decision.G2 Esports Cites Its ValuesIn a statement issued hours after Perković's post, chief executive Alban Dechelotte linked the decision to the organisation's responsibility towards its international audience. The announcement did not name Perković or specify which team he coached.'While the world is complex and not everyone agrees on everything, some of the statements made last night do not align with G2's stance and values.'G2 emphasised that its fans have different cultures and personal opinions, and that respecting that diversity was essential when representing the organisation. Dechelotte also apologised for the impact of the remarks.'We acknowledge that this statement hurt many of our fans, and we want to apologize for it.'The Post Behind G2 Esports' DecisionIn his original post, Perković explained that he wanted readers to understand his positions 'so that, at the very least, you can hate me for what I really stand for, and then that's completely fine by me.'Describing himself as a devout Catholic, he expressed firm opposition to abortion.'I cannot comprehend how people do not understand that is a murder, as life is created at conception. That is one view I will die by and never change.''I don't really do politics, nor have I even ever voted once in my life. I do have opinions, and I wish I was more educated on the topic, but the truth is I'm not, so I stay away from it,' he wrote.He described himself as no fan of either Donald Trump or Kamala Harris.Perković denied endorsing the Tate brothers or supporting Russia in its war against Ukraine. His post also distinguished his own views from those of Rodríguez Santiago, who left G2 in 2022 after sharing a video of himself at a party with Andrew Tate.Explaining why he had publicly defended the former executive, Perković pointed to support he had received earlier in his life.'Carlos believed in me when nobody else did.'He described their differences as well as that personal history, writing, 'We have a lot of different views on life.' His defence of Rodríguez Santiago, he maintained, did not amount to endorsement of the positions others had attributed to him.What Comes Next for G2 EsportsPerković subsequently published a Bible verse from Luke about being hated and excluded for religious belief. It did not directly address G2's decision or outline his professional plans.The organisation intends to rebuild its staff and roster for the next season.Dechelotte requested patience from supporters, explaining that G2 would be unable to communicate changes until free agency officially opens.

news.title: Talent agency snaps up Starmer for speaking engagements
news.text:
A celebrity talent agency has tapped former Prime Minsiter Sir Keir Starmer for speaking engagements as he looks to share his views and experiences in Downing Street at paid events. 

Starmer has signed up with Creative Artists Agency, an $1.1bn international business that counts celebrities such as Ellen DeGeneres, Gordon Ramsay, Kamala Harris and Jacinda Ardern among its clients. 

The independent adviser on ministerial standards, Sir Laurie Magnus, has provided guidance on the terms of engagement, as is routine practice for former ministers taking up roles in the private sector. 

At a recent event in Dublin, Starmer weighed in on defence matters by arguing that Europe should build a “common security framework”. He told the British Irish Chamber of Commerce dinner that the continent should “take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security”. 

Starmer’s next move

Other ministers under the Starmer government have also taken on roles in the private sector. 

Chancellor Rachel Reeves recently signed up with Chartwell Speakers. She has made a series of public appearances at university events both in the UK and across the pond in the US. 

Speaking at Harvard University this week, Reeves said her tax hikes made the UK economy “stronger” despite intense scrutiny of her economic decisions during her time in Number 11. She also took credit for offering free childcare to more parents, claiming she could support reforms by taking an economic approach through a “gender lens”. Her male predecessor, Jeremy Hunt, introduced the policy under the Conservative government. 

Starmer quit parliament just weeks after resigning as Prime Minister despite previously claiming he would not ditch his role as an MP. Reeves has not resigned as an MP. 

Sagal Abdi-Wali won his seat at Holborn and St Pancras after beating Green Party leader Zack Polanski in a by-election. 

It is unknown what Starmer’s next official role could be after a career leading the Crown Prosecution Service, rising to the top of the Labour Party and winning a huge majority in the Commons in 2024 – before leaving politics due to months of scrutiny over the state of the economy, his handling of Lord Peter Mandelson’s appointment as ambassador and ability to effect “change”.

news.title: Kamla aligned T&T's foreign policy to Trump. Now what?
news.text:
DURING her past two years in office, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has moved the country closer to the foreign policy and security agenda of the Donald Trump-led US administration, criticising its former Democratic administration while welcoming a greater US presence in the region and backing an aggressive and deadly campaign against drug trafficking in the Caribbean Sea.

Persad-Bissessar has made little attempt to conceal her affinity for the US President, at one time lauding his "fighting spirit" while later allowing the installation of a US military radar within the island territory and offering "unflinching" access to US forces in the lead-up to the military ouster of former Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.

Now, with democrats set to take control of both chambers of the US Congress after midterm elections, winning seats in states typically considered Republican-controlled, and defeating candidates endorsed by Trump himself, this alignment is set to face a new test.

The Prime Minister says the change will have little effect on her Government, or the country at large.

But while Trump remains President, retaining control of the US military and foreign policy until January 2029, a Democrat- controlled Congress will have greater power to investigate his administration, potentially attracting renewed attention to the country's overt US alignment, and its acceptance of US actions in the Caribbean Sea.

In January, a Democrat-controlled house can hold hearings, issue subpoenas and compel testimonies through its committees. Of notable interest, according to some reports in international media, is the military boat strike campaign in the Caribbean and Pacific that has thus far killed more than 240 people and drawn condemnation and scrutiny from the United Nations, Amnesty International and international legal experts.

Last September, as the US Department of Defense, led by Secretary Pete Hegseth, sought to launch lethal kinetic strikes on boats it alleged were ferrying drugs within the Caribbean Sea, Persad-Bissessar had praised the effort, calling for the US to kill all drug traffickers "violently".

She issued multiple statements praising the effort, even as the families of two Trinidadian fishermen claimed they were both killed in one such strike.

Those families, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union and the Center for Constitutional Rights, earlier this year filed a lawsuit in the US District Court for the District of Massachusetts, titled Burnley V United States, alleging their deaths were extrajudicial killings and constituted murders on the high seas-an offence that, if proven, can form part of an argument for impeachment in the case of Hegseth.

CNN reported yesterday that House Republicans are expected to vote to repudiate Hegseth as lawmaker Thomas Massie plans to trigger a vote to impeach him next week.

Persad-Bissessar's administration has maintained it had no involvement with the US strikes that continued into this year, and that none had occurred in its territory. Attorney General John Jeremie earlier this year told the public that he had sought advice on the legality of the US boat strikes from a 

Two questions asked by Jeremie were to determine whether the actions of the US in carrying out strikes against boats in international waters and (in the alternative) in the territorial waters of Trinidad and Tobago are permissible under international law, and whether the carrying-out of strikes from the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago against the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, in execution of operation Southern Spear, was lawful.

The response, the AG stated, had cleared T&T from bearing responsibility for US strikes, should they have been carried out within or nearby its territorial waters.

Asked about a potential Democrat-led investigation into the US' Executive on the boat strikes, political scientist Dr Bishu Ragoonath told the Express on Wednesday there was likely no Trinidadian involvement in the US-led operation.

"Trinidad and Tobago was nowhere involved in any of those things. T&T, as was stated in the Congressional hearings in the US, supported the US in their bringing down Maduro. Several other countries in the Caribbean granted the US permission to use airports and whatever else," he said.

"The investigation they could probably do is whether there was any direct evidence before the US Navy and whoever else fired those missiles. Bear in mind Trinidad and Tobago did not fire any missiles. Be mindful that we do not put ourselves into that realm that we were part of any decision-making on those strikes. That is certainly not the case," he added.

The UNC and the US

Persad-Bissessar's alignment with a Republican agenda preceded her election in 2025. In 2024, as opposition leader, she issued a statement vehemently criticising a former Democrat-led administration for what she said was a "woke extreme far left agenda".

That year, she congratulated a newly re-elected President Trump, commending his "resilience, commitment and fighting spirit, calling the former Joe Biden-Kamala Harris administration a "disaster" for the American people.

Her release claimed the Democrat-led administration "offended basic common sense and morality, overturned the norms of civilised public life, disoriented and mutilated children, censored and cancelled dissenting views, disparaged religious and conservative values, fuelled wars around the world, weaponised the judicial system against political opponents and increased nepotism, corruption, crime, poverty, homelessness and wealth inequality".

Persad-Bissessar also echoed some Grand Ole Party (GOP) positions in the lead-up to the April 2025 general election.

She called for citizens' increased access to guns, returning religion to schools, and promised migrant deportations and stricter policies.

Post-election, her Government's overt US alignment came amid a US military build-up in the Caribbean Sea and a military operation authorised by Trump to unseat Maduro.

After offering US forces access to the country's territory in the event of a Venezuelan attack on Guyana, her Government hosted the US military guided missile destroyer USS Gravely on its shores-an act that prompted Venezuela to sever its gas ties with the country and declare her persona non grata. In December 2025, the Government further permitted the installation of a US military-grade air defence radar in Tobago and allowed US military aircraft to make use of its airports.

The radar was removed earlier this year. In March, Persad-Bissessar attended the Shield of the Americas Summit hosted by Trump, aligning the country with the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition that she said would strengthen the country's fight against guns and drugs.

In February, as the US intensified pressure on Cuba, ramping up efforts to block the transportation of sanctioned Venezuelan oil to the country, Persad-Bissessar declared the country did not support what she referred to as a "dictatorial" regime in Cuba.

Weeks later, as the US began operation Epic Fury in Iran, killing its former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and kick-starting a weeks-long war in the Middle East, Trinidad and Tobago again expressed support for the US.

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said it supported continued actions of the US aimed at "preventing oppressive regimes from acquiring nuclear weapons capabilities that would jeopardise international peace and security. The proliferation of such weapons is a grave threat to the global community".

The country moved to officially designate Hezbollah, Hamas and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as terrorist entities.

More recently, as her Government broke its historical precedent of voting in favour of a UN resolution to end the US' embargo on Cuba, it also abstained from a resolution backing the International Criminal Court, amid US scrutiny of the international institution.

Uncritical support for Trump

Former permanent representative to the UN and former UNC MP Rodney Charles issued a statement in the aftermath of the elections on Wednesday, calling for the country to "stop taking embarrassingly unpopular positions on the global stage".

This, he said, included posters on the Cuban embargo, the ICC, the Caribbean remaining a zone of peace and alleged involvement in the domestic affairs of Venezuela and what he said was the country's possible co-conspiratorial role in alleged extra-judicial killings in Caribbean waters. "The list goes on and on, inspired by seemingly uncritical support for an unpopular President Trump. Absent a course correction, we may well find ourselves isolated on the global stage, largely ignored, and possibly a pariah state. We cannot continue forever to side with the minority at the UN, in Caricom and other global fora," he said.

He said the country is now aligned with a most unpopular US administration and that congressional investigations could reveal alleged roles in Maduro's removal and in alleged extrajudicial killings in Caribbean waters.

"My advice? Get legal advice ASAP on how to deal with the ICC-if issues arise. Former president Anthony Carmona, who sat as a judge on the Bench, seems eminently qualified to do so. Not some expensive King's Counsel. Get PR advice on how to handle setbacks resulting from congressional hearings. Do damage control with Democrats through off-ramp and other diplomatic initiatives," he wrote.

"Set up a group of professionals, here and abroad, and involve bodies like UWI to help develop well thought out policies (which could become the basis for Green Papers) on various foreign policy challenges. Discuss these in caucus, with the wider public, and in Parliament. Let the entire country 'reason together' on foreign policy issues," he added.
news.summary: DURING her past two years in office, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar has moved the country closer to the foreign policy and security agenda of the Donald Trump-led US administration, criticising its former Democratic administration while welcoming a greater US presence…

news.title: ‘I didn’t expect to be a main character’: Abdul El-Sayed heads to the Senate with a mandate – and a spotlight
news.text:
Abdul El-Sayed said he did not expect to be “a main character of this midterms”, but the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history will take his seat in January after a vitriolic campaign that cast him as the central villain of the president and his party.

By October he told the Associated Press he was “not shying away” from those rightwing fixations. “What are you implying?” El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, replied when a town hall attender asked if he would disavow the Muslim Brotherhood, in a now-viral exchange.

On Tuesday, Michigan voters helped the pugnacious progressive cap off a transcendental blue wave nationwide, defeating his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, by about seven points, 52.5% to 45.5%.

“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed,” he said at the beginning of his victory speech in downtown Detroit on Tuesday night, as the crowd erupted in cheers. He then thanked the voters of Michigan, for taking a “chance on the unlikeliest of candidates”.

He won with majorities among Black voters and Jewish early voters, and with a larger share of the vote than Kamala Harris or senator Elissa Slotkin in 2024 in Wayne, Oakland and Macomb counties, despite Republican attacks on his faith and objections from some Jewish leaders to his stance on Israel. Now he takes that mandate to Washington as one of the most visible Democrats to have emerged from this election cycle.

“He is a charismatic, social media-savvy politician, so he will come to DC with a lot more initial interest than most freshman politicians,” said Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research. “He won’t be able to say he had some sort of unique vision that worked above all others, but he will be able to say people said he couldn’t win in a swing state, and he did. I think that will matter.”

The test, according to Shekar Narasimhan, founder and chair of the AAPI Victory Fund, a Super Pac focused on Asian American and Pacific Islander political power, is less about identity than delivery.

“I think the onus on Abdul is less about being the first Muslim senator. Obviously, there is a weight for that, but it’s more about how he represents Michigan given the $165m that was thrown at him in both the primary and the general election,” Narasimhan said. “I think he does have to carry an agenda, and I think the caucus is going to give him some leadership position to be able to carry it out.”

For many Arab and Muslim Americans, the result was vindication. Maya Berry, executive director of the Arab American Institute, called voters’ rejection of the attacks on El-Sayed “tremendous” for “every little boy named Abdul, every little girl named Zainab”, arguing that the question at stake was whether the country supports an inclusive democracy.

Donald Trump and other Republicans repeatedly used Islamophobia to target his faith. At a rally in Port Huron on 25 October, the president baselessly called El-Sayed a jihadist and a Muslim Brotherhood member, said he was “on the side of the terrorists”, and claimed he would “have to go through a metal detector” before entering the Senate. John Kennedy, the senator from Louisiana, said El-Sayed “sleeps in a Bin Laden jersey”, while Ted Cruz, the senator from Texas, called him a “jihadist leprechaun”, and JD Vance called him “evil”.

Campaign mailers paid for by the Senate Leadership Fund, a prominent Republican Super Pac, and seen by the Guardian would link El-Sayed with Sharia law, with text that said his specific views “dictates how women dress”, “requires women have a guardian” and “prohibits women from divorcing”.

El-Sayed dismissed those attacks, quipping that he supported “shawarma law”.

On election night, Dearborn’s mayor, Abdullah Hammoud, said voters chose El-Sayed “regardless of the direction in which he prays”. He called it “a beautifully American story”.

Some Jewish leaders, such as the Detroit community director for the American Jewish Committee, Amy Sapeika, said El-Sayed’s rhetoric, and even his victory speech, made many in the community “feel excluded as Jews and as people who support Israel”.

While exit polls and preliminary analyses show that a majority of Michigan Jews voted for El-Sayed, his margins in heavily Jewish communities trailed other Democrats in the state, such as the governor-elect, Jocelyn Benson. In West Bloomfield, where a synagogue attack took place in March, Rogers’s share of the vote rose to 46% from 42% two years ago, when he ran against Slotkin for the Senate.

El-Sayed would reach the same parity with Black voters as Slotkin’s win in 2024, where he won about 86% compared to her 85%, according to an exit poll by NBC.

On Israel, El-Sayed has not changed his position since being elected. On election day morning, Trump said on Fox & Friends that roughly $4bn in annual US military aid to Israel would be “cut off at the end of the year”, citing “lunatics like an El-Sayed”. El-Sayed, who campaigned on ending the aid, welcomed the announcement and called for an end to arms sales as well.

While Congress appropriates the aid, Grossmann said Trump had “basically credited Abdul with changing his position on aid to Israel”, giving him an early win. Narasimhan called the announcement “a good starting point”. He said efforts by Bernie Sanders and other Democrats to restrict offensive weapons were “as far as he’s going to get in this environment on Israel”.

Asked on CNN on Thursday about working with the president and vice-president, El-Sayed made clear he was not softening his tone. He said he would “take every opportunity” to “differentiate between what JD Vance says and what JD Vance does”, and that he finds the pair “odious” in how they behave outside their official roles.

But he also said he would work with them. “I’ll work with anybody to serve the people of the state of Michigan,” he said. “If they’re serious about doing that, let’s get some stuff done.”

The successful Democratic contender for a Michigan Senate seat parried the many insinuations lobbed by Republicans

Abdul El-Sayed said he did not expect to be “a main character of this midterms”, but the first Muslim elected to the US Senate in history will take his seat in January after a vitriolic campaign that cast him as the central villain of the president and his party.

news.title: The Patriot Post® · More Than a Thumping, Possibly a Realignment
news.text:
More than a “thumping.” That’s what George W. Bush called it when Democrats won majorities in both houses by gaining six Senate and 30 House seats in 2006. In Tuesday’s midterm elections, Democrats won majorities in both houses, gaining seven Senate seats, with chances at two more, and have gained or are ahead in 40 Republican House seats.

Quite a reversal from 2024. As Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini notes, President Donald Trump’s party may end up holding no House seat that voted for Trump by less than 9 points two years ago.

Trump likes to boast that he carried all seven target states in his 50% to 48% popular-vote reelection. This year, all seven — Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin — went Democratic.

Much — maybe nearly all — of this is Trump’s doing. His “Liberation Day” tariffs, and the frivolous way he kept adjusting tariffs up and down, clearly kept inflation up and produced no visible positive effect. Like Joe Biden’s belief in Democrats’ historic remedy of pump-priming spending, Trump’s idiosyncratic belief in the power of tariffs proved destructive for his standing and his party’s.

Trump’s insistence on slavish loyalty in selecting candidates has also cost Republicans dearly. His choices in Georgia (2021 and 2022) and Arizona (2020 and 2024), his failure to get candidates who lost by less than 1 percentage point across the finish line in Wisconsin and Michigan in 2024, and his picks this year in North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas have arguably cost the party nine Senate seats heading into 2027.

That’s the difference between a Democratic Senate with 54 or 55 seats and a Republican Senate with the same majority. Between a Senate that confirms Republican Supreme Court nominees and one that invokes the Mitch McConnell precedent to refuse even to consider them. Between a Senate that might seriously consider convicting and removing an impeached president and one that would reject the effort outright.

As always, small numbers can make big differences in a 100-member Senate. Odds tend to prevail in elections for all 435 House members. And overall, the numbers in the public polls have held up pretty well this year, as pollsters have been making reasonable adjustments to lower response rates from Republicans — a subject on which I may comment later, and many others will soon.

And the messages from comparisons between the 2026 exit poll and 2024 exit poll stack up pretty well with the county election reports pouring in over the last 24 hours.

Republican percentages this year seem to be about 6 percentage points lower than Trump’s 2024 percentages among the most watched demographic groups — whites, men and women, white college graduates and non-graduates, and various income groups.

In the county returns, we see central-city counties post overwhelming Democratic percentages, suggesting a sweep of almost every precinct. We see Republican majorities in suburban and exurban counties atrophying in the Southeast and disappearing in Texas. We see Republican percentages holding up only in the most un-metropolitan rural counties.

We see some interesting regional patterns. In far northern states, Republican candidates for senator and governor did not lag as far behind Trump’s 2024 levels, perhaps for local reasons: Sen. Susan Collins’s (R-Maine) personal popularity, Democratic scandals in Minnesota, and Abdul El-Sayed’s divisiveness in Michigan kept Democrats from running more than 1, 3 and 4 points ahead of Kamala Harris.

In contrast, Democratic Senate candidates ran 11 points ahead of Harris in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia and 7 points ahead in Florida. We see here that the slow and steady movement of Northeasterners down I-95 and I-85 over the years has made the South Atlantic states, at least this year, the scene of close partisan battles, just as the once-Republican states in the Northeast became in the wake of the New Deal three generations ago. The biggest surprise was the Democratic victories in South Carolina, which had the nation’s fastest percentage population growth in 2025 to 2026.

Note also that nationally, there were significant Republican declines, by double digits, among Hispanics, Asians and “others” — groups among which Trump posted gains in 2024. Hispanics and Asians voted about 27% Republican in 2012 and 2016, 46% and 40% Republican, respectively, in 2024, and 35% and 29%, respectively, in 2026. Similarly, voters aged 18 to 29 showed increasing support for Trump in 2024 and sharply reduced levels in 2026.

This decline in Republican support wreaked havoc with the party’s efforts, urged on by Trump, to draw new congressional district lines in Republican-controlled states. These inspired similar efforts by Democrats, which in California proved successful, while declining Republican percentages among Hispanics produced “dummymanders” that backfired, especially in Texas and North Carolina. In the latter, House Republican campaign committee chairman Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.) lost his seat — the first such loss I can recall since House Democratic campaign chairman James Corman lost in the San Fernando Valley in 1980.

Will those 2024 gains turn out to be a onetime phenomenon? Or do they remain harbingers of a possible future? No one knows for sure, and voters themselves are poor prognosticators of their own future attitudes. But I suspect the big drop among these volatile groups — Hispanics and Asians tend to be younger than average — can be explained by a sense that the second-term Trump hasn’t lived up to his basic campaign promise.

His most effective 2024 ad, as I wrote three weeks ago, showed video of Harris emphasizing her support for government-paid surgery for transgender prison inmates, with the tagline, “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you.” He underlined that message visually by working a McDonald’s fry station and a drive-through window in the target state of Pennsylvania.

Trump’s conduct since November 2024 has undermined his “cares about people like me” message. Tariffs and military action against Iran and in the Gulf of Hormuz suggested an indifference to the inflationary pain they seemed to cause ordinary people. The new White House ballroom, the triumphal arch (with military uses) and his threat to demolish the Kennedy Center unless his name was put on it suggested a preoccupation with celebrating himself that was capped by his election-eve address at the Reflecting Pool, inviting comparison with the mythical Narcissus, who couldn’t stop looking at his own reflection.

These are personal flaws, but they damaged a party he has battered into subservience. They benefited an opposition party that most voters, polls show, view negatively and expect little from — and whose hold on twentysomethings, Hispanics, Asians and other more volatile voting groups remains uncertain.

This year’s vote is an attempt to put limits on the actions and vagaries of a disappointing incumbent president. It is not atypical of our era of polarized political parity, in which, in seven of the last nine presidential elections, voters have given the winner’s party trifectas — control of the presidency, Senate and House — and in six of those seven cases have withdrawn the trifecta in the off-year election two years later.

Are we looking at the beginning of a political realignment? Toward some period of Democratic dominance rather than the two-party parity we’ve enjoyed (or endured) since 1994? RealClearPolitics analyst Sean Trende, author of what I consider the best book on the 1952-92 alignment, “The Lost Majority,” tweeted on election night, “Just understand that you’re seeing something special, a 100-year flood. Easily the worst election for a party since 1974.”

I’m not so sure. It could turn out to be, but that depends on political decisions that have not yet been made and exogenous events (macroeconomic trends, technological advance, wars) that have not yet occurred. This year’s results sit just at the outer limits of the two-party parity we have enjoyed (or endured) since the presidential election of 1992 and the congressional elections of 1994.

Democrats have dominated the presidency, narrowly, winning four of seven elections, with an average popular vote margin of 49% to 46%. That’s significantly narrower than Republicans’ 52%-to-45% average popular vote margin in the 10 elections from 1952 to 1988. In seven of those 10 elections, one party won more than 53% of the popular vote. Since then, no one has; Barack Obama came closest with 52.9% in 2008.

The 1992 election that brought Bill Clinton to the White House also gave Democrats their 40th year in control of the House of Representatives by a 258-to-176 margin. Democrats had won at least 243 seats in every election since 1958. Neither party has won 258 House seats since, and only twice in 30 years has either party (Democrats in 2008, Republicans in 2014) won more than 243. Democrats this year are topping 243 but will not reach 257, as they did in 2008, or top the 258 that for decades was the party’s norm.

In the 16 Senate elections starting in 1994, Republicans have ended up with majorities in 10 and Democrats in six, with the votes split almost evenly. Only once, and for only eight months, did either party have a 60-vote filibuster-proof majority: Democrats from July 2009, when Al Franken was sworn in as winner of the contested Minnesota race, until February 2010, when Scott Brown was sworn in after winning the special election to replace Edward Kennedy.

Other than during that Congress, neither party has emerged from an election with more than 55 seats, a level Republicans reached in 1996 and 1998 and Democrats reached in 2012 and will reach again if, as is unclear at this writing, they win either of the seats up this year in Alaska and Mississippi, and will exceed if they win both.

Democrats’ House and Senate margins this week look impressive by the standards of 1994-2026, though ordinary by those of 1952-90. Do they signal the start of an extended period of political dominance, like the 36 years Republicans enjoyed after their landslide in 1894? That election overturned the 218-124 Democratic majority elected two years earlier and produced a 253-93 Republican supermajority. History offers some perspective, but this is a topic for another day.

news.title: After the midterms, the global right is reeling. But the danger of Trumpism will never be gone | Jonathan Freedland
news.text:
He’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad.

Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats in the popular vote for the House of Representatives was greater even than the 11.2% swing recorded in the Watergate midterms of November 1974, following the resignation in disgrace of Richard Nixon. Trump had worked hard for many months to undermine these elections, either by gerrymandering districts in his favour or preparing the ground for a later claim the vote was rigged, but to no avail: the democratic system proved too resilient, and the American public too determined to have their say. And have it they did, in a voice loud and clear.

Beyond the US, the temptation will be strong to see this as the moment the wheels came off the authoritarian, nationalist populist bandwagon that has rolled through so much of our politics this past decade. Viktor Orbán’s fall in April was pivotal, but the humiliation of Trump was always going to matter more. Thanks to the sheer might of the US, Trump has for a decade been the engine of the illiberal international. And now it is sputtering.

All that is cause for delight. But the risk is that those who have fought nationalist populism will take Tuesday’s success as their cue to relax. That would be to repeat the mistake made by Trump himself – and too many others – in November 2024, when he interpreted his win over Kamala Harris not as the cry of a public fed up with rising grocery bills and petrol prices, but as a permanent “vibe shift” in the culture and a mandate to turn the US into an autocracy, take a chainsaw to US government agencies, have masked men abduct and shoot American citizens on the streets, launch a doomed and disastrous war, and fill the US capital with monuments to his own vanity, all while lining his pockets and those of his inner circle.

The equivalent error this time, whether it’s made inside or outside the US, would be to read these midterm results as the end of the Trump threat and as proof that normal service will resume shortly. The danger of Trumpism, sadly, will never be gone. Because if something can happen once, it can happen again. Trump was possible – which means another Trump is possible.

That is the lesson the US’s traditional allies, in Britain, the EU or elsewhere, need to internalise. Even if Capitol Hill will soon be in saner hands, even if Trump’s eventual successor is a good internationalist who believes in a rules-based order, the reliability of the US as an ally can never again be taken for granted. After Trump, the US’s status as a guarantor of western security is anything but guaranteed, contingent instead on this or that election result. Which means that the rest of the west must still plan for its own protection and defence.

Sure, nationalist populism is now badly damaged, marked as the cause of losers. What’s more, Trump may well have demonstrated that nationalist movements whose sole currency is grievance will ultimately always fail – thereby deterring voters in France and Germany tempted to vote for Marine Le Pen or the AfD.

But, again, it’s hard to rely on that. Did Trump fail because politicians of his ilk always will? Or was it because he made stupid and, crucially, avoidable decisions, such as attacking Iran – which not only broke his core pledge, so cherished by Maga voters, to end wars rather than start them, but also drove up the very inflation he was elected to curb? Either way, it’s hard to speak of inevitable failure when describing a man who, despite all the havoc he wreaked the first time around – including the violent insurrection of 6 January 2021 – was elected to a fresh term less than four years later. He disgraced himself, but was rewarded with victory.

Besides, it’s too soon to speak of Trump in the past tense. True, he’s lost the doormat House and the rubber-stamp Senate that enabled him to act without restraint. But a weakened Trump is not necessarily a tamed Trump. I think of the seasoned Washington hand who told me Trump in defeat could become “a cornered animal”. When it comes to the world stage, he still has the power to act – foreign policy is largely the preserve of the president – and a double motive to do so. First, he will want a legacy to offset this week’s historic drubbing and, second and even more elementally, he craves the attention. The notion of ceding the spotlight to Democrats, or in fact anyone, will appal him.

Maybe he will bow to the demands lodged by JD Vance - in a statement on X that saw the vice president all but break from his boss – and move to end the war with Iran, even if that means capitulation. Or he might double down and push for the toppling of the Tehran regime that he likely believes would give him the place in history he deserves.

Until 20 January 2029 those decisions will be Trump’s. He still has the power to shape world events, even if that power has diminished. Take as just one example, the US relationship with Israel. That country had elections of its own last week that, though far from delivering the repudiation of Benjamin Netanyahu many Israelis sought, did wipe out his parliamentary majority. Coalition horsetrading is now under way, and the US midterms are already playing a part. Israeli opposition leaders argue that what Netanyahu long claimed as an asset – his closeness to Trump – is, after Tuesday, a liability, rendering Israel’s prime minister “toxic” among the Democrats who will soon wield power on Capitol Hill. If that argument prevails, the blue tsunami will have claimed not only Kansas and Texas, but the man once dubbed the Republican senator from Jerusalem.

On the morning of election day, Trump announced the termination of military aid to Israel, perhaps in a last-ditch attempt to win over Tucker Carlson Republicans who are hostile to the country. He could continue on that path, especially if he seeks to punish Netanyahu for his role in the joint US-Israeli war on Tehran that broke his presidency or, alternatively, he could defy Vance and hug the Israeli PM close.

The point is, these fateful choices still rest with Trump. Democrats will soon have the power to investigate allegations of corruption and hold him to account. America’s allies in Europe and elsewhere will soon find in Washington people who talk like partners, rather than enemies. Both prospects come as a great relief. But that does not alter two key facts: Trump happened – and he’s still there.

 Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
news.summary:
Yes, the Republicans suffered humiliating defeat. But the fact that a Trump presidency was even possible means something like it could happen again

He’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad.

Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats

news.title: ‘Son-in-law of Karnataka’: Abdul el-Sayed’s Indian side of family celebrates US midterms win
news.text:
Family members of Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed in India are celebrating his victory in the US midterm elections after he beat Republican Mike Rogers following a bitter campaign in one of the most important swing states.

Dr El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, is married Sarah Jukaku, a practicing psychiatrist with roots in India's southern state of Karnataka.

The couple met during their time at the University of Michigan and subsequently got married in 2006, according to reports. 

While Dr Jukaku was born and raised in Michigan, her relatives still live in Bhatkal, around 490km west of state capital, Bengaluru.

Jukaku Abdul Majeed, a Kerala-based businessman and uncle of Dr Jukaku, said Dr El-Sayed's victory was a deeply personal triumph.

"Muslims constitute only around 2.5 per cent of the US population. We never imagined that the outcome would be in his favour, given the circumstances. His victory came as a blessing," he told the New Indian Express.

Family members called Dr El-Sayed the “son-in-law of Karnataka” and a warm and approachable person. 

The couple, who share two daughters, had travelled to Bhatkal over a decade ago to attend a cousin's wedding, spending at least four days with the family.

Dr Jukaku's cousin Bibi Husna told NDTV that the family was stressed during the fierce campaign and on the counting day. "But by the grace of God, it has been a lovely victory," she said.

Mr El-Sayed, during his campaign, quipped that being married to a South Indian woman for two decades had made him "more Indian than Arab". "Everybody likes desis more than Arabs," he said on a podcast.

He added: "I'm an honorary Indian. There is a patience to Indian culture that I appreciated only when I went to India. You're surrounded by a billion people. Nothing gets done quickly," he added.

In another podcast posted in August, he recalled that his uncle asked him why he married an Indian when there were 80 million Egyptians. Dr El-Sayed responded, saying: "Amu (uncle in Arabic), there are a billion of them, so statistically speaking, this was a high probability."

Mr El-Sayed separately said he was "surrounded by desi women... I have two desi daughters and a desi wife".

Dr Jukaku's father, Jukaku Tayeb, studied at the Bangalore Medical College before moving to the US in 1976. Her grandfather, Jukaku Shamshuddin, served as deputy minister for finance in the erstwhile Mysore state.

Mr El-Sayed has also often spoken fondly about his heritage, praised Egyptian food and humour, and warmly recalled summers in the Mediterranean city of Alexandria, where his father grew up.

Mr El-Sayed is a former public health official who focused his grassroots campaign on universal health care, removing outside money from elections, and sharp criticism of Israel. It carried him past massive outside spending in both the Democratic primary and the general election.

His victory will bolster the movement ahead of the 2028 presidential election, offering evidence that candidates embracing its agenda can win in critical battleground states.

Former president Barack Obama and former vice president Kamala Harris were among the high-profile Democrats who campaigned with El-Sayed in the city to help mobilise voters.
news.summary: Relatives call El-Sayed the ‘son-in-law of Karnataka’

news.title: Democrats Gearing Up For 2028 Presidential Elections To Gain Full Power
news.text:
By T N Ashok

NEW YORK: The November 3 midterm elections have given the Democrats an extraordinary opportunity to reclaim the political initiative in Washington. But the victory carries a warning of its own: the electorate may have voted against Donald Trump, but it has not necessarily handed the Democratic Party an unconditional mandate. Its immediate challenge is to demonstrate that it can make everyday American life more affordable.

The central political question following the Democratic triumph is no longer simply how badly the Republicans have been punished. It is whether the Democrats can translate an electoral revolt into an economic recovery before the presidential election of 2028.

For millions of Americans, the ballot was a verdict on the cost of living, the price of petrol, grocery bills, employment insecurity, immigration enforcement, visa restrictions, healthcare costs and the economic consequences of Trump’s tariffs and the war with Iran. The concerns of ordinary households, rather than the ideological arguments of Washington, became the defining issues of the election.

The Democrats must therefore resist the temptation to treat their victory as an invitation to settle every political score with Trump. Their first responsibility is to the voters who gave them this opportunity.

Former president Barack Obama, whose campaigning helped Democrats make inroads into states once considered safely Republican, offered perhaps the most useful framework for understanding the result. He said the American people had “sent a clear message” and wanted politics that brought people together rather than divided them, alongside leaders capable of delivering concrete solutions. He urged Democrats to roll up their sleeves, make changes where they had the power, prevent further damage and prepare for the future.

That is a more consequential message than the celebrations surrounding the election-night results. Obama understands that a midterm victory can be squandered if a party mistakes rejection of its opponents for unconditional support of its own programme. His experience of the 2010 midterms, when Republicans captured the House after his own sweeping victory two years earlier, offers a cautionary parallel. Voters can change their minds quickly when expectations are disappointed.

For the Democrats, the lesson is clear: the 2026 election has given them the power to obstruct, investigate and negotiate, but their credibility by 2028 will depend on whether they can improve the lives of people who supported them.

The new majority must therefore establish a governing agenda that can survive partisan warfare. Its priorities should include reducing the cost of essential goods, strengthening access to affordable healthcare, protecting employment, improving educational affordability and addressing the consequences of the Iran conflict.

The party should also resist allowing its message to be overwhelmed by personalities and presidential ambitions. Obama, Bill Clinton and other former Democratic leaders can help build a common programme, but they cannot substitute for visible results from the politicians who now hold office.

Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer: from opposition to responsibility. For House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, poised to become speaker, the victory offers the opportunity to turn opposition into a credible legislative alternative.

Jeffries declared: “This is a change election.” He added that House Democrats understood they needed to “deliver dramatic change.”

That promise creates a demanding test. Democrats will have to decide which parts of their programme can be advanced through legislation, which can be achieved through congressional oversight and which require negotiations with Trump.

Control of both chambers gives them substantial leverage. They can investigate executive-branch decisions, scrutinise federal spending, challenge appointments and use hearings to demand answers about the administration’s conduct. But congressional control does not automatically translate into the ability to enact every policy the party favours. Presidential vetoes, Senate procedure, disagreements within the Democratic coalition and the courts will all constrain what can be achieved.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer likewise faces a transformed political landscape. Democratic victories in states previously regarded as difficult terrain for the party suggest that economic discontent has crossed traditional partisan boundaries.

Schumer’s task is to turn that geographically broad coalition into a functioning legislative majority. He must accommodate moderates concerned about deficits and business confidence, progressives demanding more expansive social programmes, and senators who may prefer incremental reforms to confrontational political theatre.

There is a strategic distinction between using congressional power to expose misconduct and using it to improve economic conditions. The two are not mutually exclusive, but they require different timetables and different measures of success.

A carefully documented investigation can establish accountability. A prolonged partisan spectacle, however, can consume months without lowering a single household bill. The Democrats would be wise to make their oversight rigorous, evidence-led and focused on matters of public importance, while ensuring that economic legislation does not disappear beneath the noise.

Former president Bill Clinton’s post-election message was direct: “You deserve a government that works as hard for you as you do for your family.” He had campaigned on lowering costs, protecting healthcare, ending senseless wars and reversing tariffs that make life more expensive. After the victory, his emphasis was on the work still to be done, rather than simply celebrating the result.

Clinton’s perspective is particularly relevant because he presided over a Democratic administration that placed considerable emphasis on economic growth, employment and fiscal credibility. His political instinct is to connect a party’s broader values with material improvements in household circumstances.

That is also the challenge facing Kamala Harris. The former vice-president, who lost the 2024 presidential election to Trump, has continued to campaign for Democratic candidates and has signalled that she wants to help shape the party’s future. Her post-election significance lies not merely in whether she seeks the nomination again, but in how she interprets the message from voters who have rejected the governing party.

Harris and other senior Democrats must resist the temptation to turn the midterm result immediately into a competition for the 2028 presidential nomination. The party needs a convincing economic programme before it needs a nominee.

There is a political danger in allowing the victory to become a contest between the progressive and moderate wings. Progressives will argue that the results validate stronger intervention on healthcare, wages, housing and corporate power. Moderates will warn that expansive promises can become liabilities if they are not adequately financed or cannot pass Congress.

Both sides have a legitimate argument. The winning formula must combine ambition with credibility: proposals that help working families, explain how they will be funded and can be translated into legislation or practical administrative action.

The Democratic victories have strengthened the position of several governors and national figures who could compete for the presidential nomination in 2028..They include apart from former Vice President Kamala Harris, California Governor Gavin Newsom, Illinois Governor J B Pritzker, Pennsylvania Democrat John Shapiro. Former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg and Leftist house representative Alexander Occasio Cortez of New York.

These figures should not be treated as though each has issued an identical post-election manifesto. Their significance is strategic: the Democrats now have several potential leaders who can claim a role in the party’s revival, but they will ultimately be judged on what they deliver.

For all five, the danger is that presidential positioning begins to overshadow governing. The electorate did not vote in November 2026 to stage a preliminary contest for the Democratic nomination. It voted to change the balance of power and, above all, to demand a different direction. .The functioning of the Democrats in the next two years within the Congress as also outside, will determine whether the blue wave of 2026 midterm can be sustained and converted into votes in 2028 presidential elections. (IPA Service)

news.title: [Whispers] The Democratic Party Is Good at Politics
news.text:
Making fun of the Democratic Party has long been a bipartisan pastime. “I don’t belong to any organized political faith. I am a Democrat,” the actor Will Rogers said in 1933. Nearly a century later, Donald Trump mocks the party as “Dumbocrats.” Democrats in disarray has become a cliché among beltway journalists. A screenshot from a 1994 episode of The Simpsons, which depicts a Democratic convention unfolding beneath slogans like “We Can’t Govern!” and “We Hate Life and Ourselves,” circulates on social media with dismal frequency. In an AP/NORC poll last year, voters described the party as “weak,” “ineffective,” and “generally bad.” And those voters were Democrats.

A similar undercurrent of belittlement is already detectable after Tuesday’s midterms, which resoundingly swept Democrats back into power in Congress, governors’ mansions, and hundreds of other seats across the country. “Will Democrats Misread Their Victory?” the Wall Street Journal wonders. “Democrats, Don’t Mess This Up,” admonishes the Intercept. The skepticism is coming from inside the (literal) House too. “I’m really worried that we’re going to misread victory as an endorsement of us or America falling in love with Democrats,” Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut told Time magazine. “We need to remember that we have been asked to audition for a role in which the party has failed.” It’s as if the whole country can’t help but picture Democrats stepping on a rake at the earliest possible opportunity.

Governing is harder than campaigning, so those concerns aren’t totally unjustified. Yet the midterm results highlight an important truth that has long gone underappreciated: Democrats really aren’t so bad at this whole politics thing. Derided on the left and right as unpopular, out-of-touch quislings, Democrats proved this week that they remain plenty adaptable, resilient, and effective at winning power. Unlike the GOP, which has been in thrall to Trumpism for a decade, and despite Americans’ growing disenchantment with political parties in general, Democrats still behave the way an effective political party should: recalibrating after defeats, adjusting messages as the political environment shifts, backing quality candidates, and tolerating a broad spectrum of ideologies and voices under one umbrella. Parties exist to win elections, and on that score this donkey remains alive and kicking.

I can hear the objections already: Didn’t Democrats fumble two presidential races against Trump? And isn’t the chief architect of the party’s midterm victories actually the president himself, who spiked prices with tariffs and a war? Yes and yes. No point in sugarcoating it: Losing to Trump not once but twice has been hugely costly, not least for the Democrats’ brand. And both times, the party made major missteps. In 2016, Democrats ignored warning signs while clearing the field for Hillary Clinton, a candidate who was a poor match for the moment. In 2024, the party did the right thing by pushing Joe Biden out of the race over widespread concerns about his age, but Dems did so too late—and paid for it dearly.

But the mark of a successful political party isn’t winning every election. In fact, adaptation after defeat is arguably the story of Democrats’ persistence. As the historian Michael Kazin writes in What It Took to Win, his 2022 history of the Democrats, “the party’s history is rife with missteps and outrages.” Yet as Kazin also notes, the party has consistently turned rejections at the ballot box into opportunities for reinvention. There’s a reason the Democrats are considered the longest continually active political party in the world; you don’t get to be 198 years old without knowing a few things about survival.

Democrats have proved that repeatedly during the Trump era, but particularly over the past two years. In 2020, Biden ran on restoring “the soul of America” and barely beat Trump. Four years later, Kamala Harris repeatedly warned that Trump threatened both American democracy and Americans’ fundamental freedoms, calling him a “petty tyrant” and “wannabe dictator.” (I don’t have to remind you what happened next.) A less disciplined party might have stuck with the same message in 2026; Trump, after all, keeps trying to imprison his political opponents, restrict voting rights, and side with foreign dictators over democratic allies. But after losing to him a second time, Democrats pivoted. Democrats blaming Trump for Americans’ ongoing concerns about affordability was a no-brainer, but Harris also lost in part because she failed to draw meaningful contrasts with Biden over issues like immigration. This year, Democratic candidates including James Talarico in Texas, Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Paige Cognetti in Pennsylvania, and even the progressive Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan blasted the Biden administration for failing to secure the southern border. Each of those candidates won. Harris’ past criticisms of oil drilling and comments about transgender Americans also came back to bite her in 2024. This year, Talarico vowed to protect his state’s fossil-fuel industry, and Andrews cut an ad saying she opposed letting trans athletes compete in women’s sports—positions that, whether one agrees with them or not, reflected the places they were trying to win. On the GOP side, politicians who break from Trump get Truth Social screeds and their careers ended by a president who endorses their primary challengers. But because Democrats are a political party rather than a cult of personality, their leaders can brook disagreements in the interest of winning power. Biden reportedly called Cognetti this week to congratulate her on her victory.

Those maneuvers may be the most dramatic examples of Democrats’ adaptability, but this week’s victories also built on wins the party notched even in years it lost the presidency. Since the Trump era began, Democrats have done a pretty good job of overcoming the Senate’s inherent bias toward Republicans, managing to net seats in traditionally red states like Georgia, Arizona, and Alabama and defend seats in purple states like Arizona, Michigan, and Nevada even as Trump won them. Democrats have now clinched resounding House majorities twice and held their losses to single digits in 2022, a midterm that took place under an unpopular, inflation-besieged president of their own party. When Trump was inaugurated in 2017, Democrats occupied just 16 governors’ mansions around the country. As of this week, they’re poised to control nearly twice that number. Not a bad record for a party that in the popular imagination can’t stop tripping over its own feet.

And where did all those winning candidates come from? Wave elections can make almost anybody look like a political genius, but this wave started building more than a year ago thanks in part to Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, and Hakeem Jeffries, his House counterpart. After Trump’s reelection, Schumer and Jeffries effectively became pain sponges for furious liberals, who derided them as strategically feckless, cringey, and out of touch. Yet their interventions helped set the conditions for Tuesday’s blue tsunami. Last year, according to the New York Times, Schumer wooed former Gov. Roy Cooper in North Carolina, former Rep. Mary Peltola in Alaska, and a Mississippi district attorney named Scott Colom to run for Senate, reportedly telling associates that he saw Mississippi in particular as a potential surprise pickup. Pundits and Republicans scoffed. “Democrats are delusional,” the leader of a GOP super PAC told the Times. On Tuesday, Cooper romped by 20 points, and both Peltola and Colom look likely to win. Unlike political movements dominated by a single, thin-skinned figure, successful political parties are elastic enough to accommodate dissent. Schumer and his deputies threw money at candidates in tough races who criticized his leadership, including El-Sayed and Maine’s Troy Jackson, placing party interests above ego. (Still, Schumer sounds confident that he’ll have the votes to become majority leader once more, and Jeffries will almost certainly become the country’s first Black speaker.)

Democrats have done something similar over the past two years in terms of legislative strategy. Liberal voters, pundits, and even members of Congress dismissed former Bill Clinton adviser James Carville as a fuddy-duddy for suggesting that Democrats “roll over and play dead” while Trump and the GOP inevitably bungled things. Yet that approach, whether it was a conscious choice or merely a result of being in the minority, largely worked. Trump’s governing mistakes—from tariffs and Iran to aggressive immigration enforcement—are arguably the biggest reasons the midterms became a rout, and Democrats capitalized on them by (mostly) getting out of the way. Elsewhere, the party picked its battles wisely. According to the Atlantic, Jeffries resisted pressure from inside his own caucus to make the 2025 government shutdown a proxy fight over Trump’s corruption and authoritarian impulses, instead focusing relentlessly on the issue of expiring healthcare tax credits. Even as Republicans let the credits expire, polls showed that Democrats won the debate. Now Jeffries is reportedly eyeing legislation to revive those subsidies.

There are plenty of caveats to this phoenix-like story of Democratic defeat followed by renewal. For one thing, the party’s brand remains tarnished, with approval ratings well below where they were even in Trump’s first term. Yet that may start to change now that the stink of loserdom is starting to lift, and the party has a raft of new leaders to buff its image. For another, no leader bats a thousand. Schumer coaxed a reluctant Gov. Janet Mills to challenge Sen. Susan Collins in Maine and backed Michigan Rep. Haley Stevens for Senate after his preferred candidates passed. Those misfires didn’t end up costing Democrats this time, but the party has narrowly lost critical Senate races in other years, like Florida in 2018 and Pennsylvania in 2024.

It’s also true that there really can be political advantages—at least temporary ones—to behaving less like a party, which demands consensus and mutual forbearance, and more like a cult of personality. Through force of will and threats of primary challenges, Trump has bent Republicans into shapes they never would have assumed a decade ago, from getting self-described tea partiers on board with two deficit-exploding tax laws to bullying most of his party into forgiving a coup attempt. Democratic voters have often been jealous of the hold Trump has over his party’s rank and file. Still, this week’s results suggest that those heavy-handed tactics can eventually backfire. (It remains to be seen whether Tuesday’s thumping will persuade enough Republicans to act less like foot soldiers in Trump’s movement and more like a political party that wants to get out from under an unpopular president.)

Last, of course, is the question many voters, journalists, and elected Democrats are already asking: Can Democrats use the congressional majorities they just won to make life better for frustrated Americans? There are real risks that infighting over Israel, debates over how far to push on healthcare reform, and other issues will derail the bonhomie. And practically speaking, there’s probably not much the party will be able to achieve legislatively as long as Trump remains in the White House. Democrats are already disagreeing about whether to prioritize accountability for Trump officials or legislation aimed at lowering the cost of living. They’re also divided over which potential standard-bearers are best positioned to win back the White House in 2028.

Yet the past may be instructive here too. “As during the heydays of the New Deal and the Great Society,” Kazin writes in his book, the Democratic Party “can taste victory consistently only if its activists, candidates, and officeholders debate their differences without one side denouncing or seeking to purge another.” Despite the party’s many shortcomings, he argues, “the Democrats remain the only electoral institution in twenty-first-century America able to help solve the serious problems facing the United States and, to a lesser degree, the rest of humanity as well.” That’s a tall order. But this week, against all odds, Democrats really did snatch an opportunity to change the country for the better, and it would be wrong to count them out. After all, they have history on their side.
news.summary: The most mocked political party in America is actually pretty good at politics.
