news.title: Calls for more in-person voting sites in Hawaii persist
news.text:
Worries over long lines of last-minute election-day voters never materialized, and the Honolulu Hale voter serv-ice center was the last one to close in the state, with one final voter casting a ballot after the 7 p.m. end of voting, according to Rex Quidilla, administrator for the Honolulu Office of Elections.

Starting in the morning, long lines of vehicles, however, did stretch along 
Beretania Street past the Hono-lulu Police Department, down Punchbowl Street and onto King Street to place voters’ filled out, mail-in ballots into drop boxes outside Hono-lulu Hale for much of Tuesday, Quidilla said.

There was an incident in front of Honolulu Hale on election night when Quidilla and two Honolulu Police Department officers had to tell a man dressed in a tan tactical vest with the word “ICE” on the back that he had to leave because he was in an area reserved for election business, including voters.

The man told Quidilla and the HPD officers that he did not plan to vote but wanted to “hang out” in front of Hono-lulu Hale, saying it was his “right.”

He never identified himself as an ICE agent and walked across the street to Kawai-hao Church, where the HPD officers told him that he was still in the zone where “electioneering” is off-limits by law.

The incident followed concerns around the country that the Justice Department would send federal agents to monitor election sites on Election Day, leading to fears that the mere presence of federal agents would deter people from voting in an election that ended with a sweeping victory for Democrats in both blue and deep red states.

Honolulu election workers had told Quidilla on election night that they worried the man in the tactical vest might be intimidating voters with his presence, Quidilla said.

Voters in the past have tried to vote while carrying campaign signs or attire emblazoned with candidates’ names, which violates rules in Hawai and across the nation against “electioneering,” by trying to sway other voters to cast their ballots in favor of one candidate or issue over another.

They’re still allowed to vote, as long as they remove any campaign attire or material, just like similar laws across the country designed to keep polling sites neutral places to vote and prevent voter intimidation.

Quidilla said the response by Honolulu Hale election workers to enforce Hawaii election laws illustrates the demands on election workers to understand voting laws and rights — while also registering voters to vote on election day, figuring out whether they are or are not registered, have or have not already voted and to provide instructions on how to properly mark ballots to ensure they are counted.

Since Hawaii embraced mail-in voting in 2020 and shut down neighborhood voting sites at schools, parks and other public facilities, there have been ongoing calls to open more voting sites across the state on election day, in addition to the two Oahu sites at Honolulu Hale and Kapolei Hale.

In Hawaii and across the country, Republicans in general prefer to vote in person on election day compared with Democrats, who generally prefer to vote early by mail.

In past elections — especially the 2024 presidential election between President Donald Trump and Vice President Kamala Harris — last-minute voters lined up by the end of the 7 p.m. voting deadline and jammed voter service centers across the state, delaying the release of election returns for hours.

By Tuesday, 45.8% of 
Hawaii’s 853,399 registered voters cast ballots, or 391,251 people.

Once again, ballots arriving by mail or at drop boxes represented the overwhelmingly majority of voters, or 373,741 of all votes cast.

By comparison, only 17,510 voters — or 2.1% — cast ballots in person early or on election day across 

The delays in reporting voting results in previous elections have only fueled calls — primarily by Republicans and election security skeptics — to open more voter service centers that are run by counties.

Camron Hurt, state director of Common Cause 
Hawai‘i, said it was actually two trained “Common Cause election protection volunteers” who first saw the man in the tactical vest and “immediately reached out to our election protection organizer, who reached out to me. I, in turn, reached out to our team in D.C. to alert them of the issue. They asked the volunteer to get a picture.”

Based on photos of actual ICE agents compared to impersonators, Common Cause lawyers in Washington, D.C., determined the man was not legitimate.

But whether the man was an actual ICE agent or not, Hurt said, “ICE should not be at our polls, period.

On election day, Common Cause had 84 trained election protection workers across the state and the incident at Honolulu Hale showed that election workers have plenty of support that would help counties operate more in-person voting sites on election day, Hurt said.

Since Oahu already opens two additional in-person voting sites in the days leading up to election day, Hurt argued that counties should open fewer in-person sites early and more on election day to encourage more in-person voting.

“That doesn’t mean polling locations in every school, but it does mean that the biggest county in the state should have more than two in-person voting locations on the day of,” Hurt said.

He remembers his “earliest political lesson” as a 4-year-old watching his father — a soldier with the 
Army’s famed 101st Airborne Division — vote and then take him to McDonald’s, where he explained the importance of voting, especially as an African American.

“He said, ‘See this uniform I’m wearing? Part of the reason I’m doing it is so that we can always do this every Election Day,’” Hurt remembered. “As an African 
American, it is a historical obligation for me to vote in person because people literally died for the right to be able to vote in person. So, I would much rather continue that legacy.”

The lack of Election Day, in-person voting sites would have been critically important this year had the U.S. Supreme Court allowed Trump and the U.S. Postal Service to go ahead with plans not to deliver mail-in ballots in states like Hawaii that refuse to turn over state voters rolls to the federal government, Hurt said.

The U.S. Constitution leaves responsibility for elections up to individual states, not the federal government.

On Sept. 14, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a lower court ruling that prevented the threat of holding up mail-in ballots from going into effect, at least for this year’s elections.

Hurt would not be surprised to see Trump make another attempt to restrict mail-in voting before the 2028 presidential election, adding another reason that Hawaii should create more in-person voting sites in each county on Election Day, he said.

At Honolulu Hale on Election Day, Common Cause helped election officials ensure free and fair voting that would be replicated if more voting sites open on Election Day around Hawaii, Hurt said.

“No voter (at Honolulu Hale) felt intimidated because Common Cause was there to do what they were supposed to do,” he said. “Elections was there to do what they’re supposed to do and the police were there to do what they’re supposed to do.”

The Common Cause election monitors were trained to be “aware of what to do in the case of certain situations,” Hurt said. “We put in systems. and thank God they worked.”

news.title: After Two Whiplash Trump Years, Democrats Have Two More to Get China Right
news.text: Donald Trump’s China policies are contradictory, veering between threats and flattery and, most recently, settling into an uncomfortable kind of détente. That has been evidenced by razzmatazz summits with Chinese leader Xi Jinping where not much gets discussed. Xi is said to loathe meeting him or even meeting his eye, despite Trump’s avowals of friendship. In fact, for two years, Trump has flip-flopped; for example, onshoring semiconductor production on national security grounds, then selling national security-sensitive semiconductors hand over fist to China, all at the same time. His defenders say that China has the U.S. over a barrel because of its control of the rare earths that drive high-tech industry. They argue that Trump is above all buying time until the U.S. can establish its own supplies of the mining and processing of the minerals—or face losing its industrial power and sovereignty. There’s a lot of truth to that. China is perhaps America’s single most important, long-term foreign policy challenge, due to its industrial might and ambition. This dwarfs any other country’s—despite the far noisier issue, among the electorate, of the Middle East. Flush with their midterms victory, where do the Democrats stand on China, and can they work it out before 2028, when they have a serious chance of taking power? Should they critique Trump’s détente, as evidenced, for example, by his delay in supplying weapons to Taiwan and his rush to supply chips to China? Or should they lean into these policies? China barely figured in the elections. That may be a good thing for the Democrats. The range of opinion in the party is great, from the "left left" Democratic Socialists who are still few, but who exert upward pressure, are strong in the grassroots and among young people, many of whom believe that China is "anti-imperialist" even though it operates assimilationist policies toward millions of its own ethnic minorities and in border regions such as Tibet, Xinjiang where the Uyghurs live, Inner Mongolia and Hong Kong. Then there are the Democratic centrists, some would say the realists, some of them alums of the former administration of President Joe Biden. They view China as a serious national security challenge, and, when in power, worked for export controls for sensitive national security-connected technologies such as semiconductors that outstripped anything by Trump’s Department of Commerce under Howard Lutnick, but who moved more slowly against endemic espionage by China, apparently more worried about being accused of racism than combating the Communist Party's political warfare. Positioned opposite the realists is a progressive wing that believes, not so secretly, that China needs to be more or less appeased, or America risks war. For example, over Taiwan. Or that the U.S. needs to import EVs from China to combat climate change, regardless of how this will weaken it industrially. 2028 is still too far off to tell where the pieces of this debate will fall. But key people are likely keen to be part of any future Democratic administration. People like Rush Doshi, a senior China and Taiwan national security official in the Biden administration, who has been effective and critical of the CCP. Or Jessica Chen Weiss, a professor of China studies at Johns Hopkins SAIS and a former senior adviser to the State Department’s policy planning staff. She is known for advancing arguments that play down possible responses to China's challenges to the U.S., or to the status quo in the Pacific including Taiwan. Those two stand pretty much opposite each other and the contest between their visions of China policy will likely be decisive. Capturing much of this, an authoritative essay is making the rounds among China wonks titled The Fight for the Future of Democratic Foreign Policy, published on November 3 in Foreign Affairs magazine. "The midterm elections mark the beginning of the Democratic Party’s 2028 presidential campaign," writes Thomas Wright. He is a senior Fellow at the Brookings Institution and was the senior director for strategic planning at the National Security Council during the Biden administration. "After two years of debate over the lessons of Kamala Harris’ defeat in the 2024 election, it promises to be one of the most open contests about the future of Democratic policies, including foreign policy, in generations. It also promises to be one of the most consequential. The strategic environment in 2029 is on track to be the most difficult and unforgiving since the height of the Cold War," Wright writes. He has some advice: "Democrats must therefore lay out their ideas early and see how they fare both with voters and against the trajectory of world events." Failing to work out the "centrist-progressive debate," the Democrats risk being unprepared for the world of 2029, which will be a tougher place, geopolitically-speaking, than ever before, Wright says. That debate takes place roughly on the Doshi-Chen Weiss axis. Still, before they get to any of that, Democrats have a very long list of challenges they want to confront Trump with; starting with corruption, affordability, aggressive enforcement of immigration policies, his Russia policy, bullying of allies, and the Iran war. For now, China remains way down the list. That may be lucky, as they don’t have a consensus on what to do, yet.
news.summary: As Democrats emerge from two years of Trumpism, some are looking to the 2028 presidential election. That will need a China policy.

news.title: Republicans lose Congress, but Trumpism is far from finished
news.text:
The Republicans have suffered a crushing defeat in the US midterm elections, and the Democrats have every reason to celebrate, but the real significance of the result lies less in the number of seats changing hands than in what it reveals about the direction of American politics.

The warning signs were there long before polling day, given almost two years after Donald Trump’s return to the White House many Americans have seen little improvement in their daily lives. Trade wars have unsettled the economy, while the adventure in Iran has reinforced the feeling that Washington is leading the country towards another costly and unnecessary confrontation. Democrats exploited these anxieties effectively, while Trump’s coalition appeared increasingly divided and considerably less eager to defend its president than it was in 2024.

The uncertainty before the vote concerned the scale of the Republican defeat. Would the party lose the House of Representatives but cling on to the Senate, and could it preserve its advantage among state governors? In the event, the worst outcome materialized as Democrats won both chambers of Congress and, for the first time since 2010, emerged with more governorships than their rivals.

It would be easy to overstate the immediate consequences because American politics has always been capable of dramatic reversals. Even Texas, long considered a Republican fortress, has been experiencing demographic and political changes for years and nor will a Democratic Congress necessarily transform the way Trump governs. He relied heavily on executive orders when Republicans controlled Capitol Hill and is unlikely to abandon that habit now.

There will be investigations and endless talk of impeachment, and Democrats may well pursue it, but winning control of Congress isn’t the same as possessing the votes required to remove a president. Washington will find ways to keep itself busy and much of the country will carry on much as before, thus the more interesting conclusions are political rather than procedural.

First, Trump is entering the final two years of his presidency in a position weaker than that of an ordinary lame duck as he risks becoming a liability to the very Republicans who once regarded his endorsement as the surest route to office.

After losing to Joe Biden in 2020, Trump retained his influence through the image of a man persecuted by the ‘deep state’. Younger conservatives competed for his favor, while former critics, including figures such as Marco Rubio and J.D. Vance, made their peace with him. The rewards were obvious because to secure Trump’s backing was often to secure a political future.

Now that calculation looks rather different, given several candidates associated with him have been defeated, and ambitious Republicans must consider how to build careers in a post-Trump party while Trump himself remains at its center, so the contest for 2028 has acquired a complication for which there is no easy solution.

Second, the Democrats have rediscovered a political resource they badly lacked in 2024, with credible new faces. Two years ago, their inability to offer voters a more compelling alternative than Kamala Harris exposed the exhaustion of the party’s leadership, but today they can point to a younger generation of politicians, many still under 50, with the ambition and energy to compete nationally.

They’re not yet ready-made presidential candidates and they need experience in government and recognition beyond their own states, but the pool is there, and that’s already a considerable improvement.

More revealing is how these rising Democrats speak. Some have begun borrowing themes once associated almost exclusively with the right, about protecting American livelihoods, looking after problems at home rather than crusading abroad, and restoring the country’s sense of national purpose. The vocabulary has changed because the electorate has changed. Americans don’t support politicians solely for their programs, rather they also respond to the emotions those politicians awaken.

For the moment, Democrats have proved better at capturing the public mood, but whether they can translate that mood into a coherent program is quite another question.

Third, anyone expecting a simple return to pre-Trump America is likely to be disappointed. Trump’s opponents at home and abroad may interpret the Republican collapse as proof that MAGA has been defeated and the old political order can be restored, but that’s wishful thinking.

Only two years ago, conservatives greeted Trump’s victory over Harris as the final repudiation of American liberalism. Liberals are now tempted to make the same mistake in reverse, but the most reliable law of American politics is that no victory is permanent and no defeat final.

More importantly, Trump has spent a decade reshaping the country’s political arguments, so even politicians who reject him must respond to the questions he forced onto the agenda. news.title: Decoding Indian American vote in midterms: The pendulum that swings on policy, not identity
news.text:
US President Donald Trump's crackdown on immigration and the racist attacks by Republican Party members did not bode well with Indian-Americans, and this was reflected in how they voted in the 2026 US midterm elections. Traditionally, the Indian-American section of the US population has always had a leaning towards the Democrats.
However, the tide turned in the Republican Party's favour in 2024, when a significant chunk of the ethnic group backed Trump for the presidency over then Vice President Kamala Harris. Trump's promises of tax breaks, economic gains, and his overall charisma attracted the Indian-Americans who have been the prime example of "living the American dream".
But things changed when Trump came to power and unleashed one of the strictest immigration crackdowns. Many at that time raised concerns over the fact that while Trump pledged to take action against illegal immigrants, his policies are affecting legal ones as well.
Comprehensive pre-election data from the 2026 US midterm elections reveals that the community has swung decisively back into the Democratic column. Driven by intense anxieties over the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration overhauls and a wave of defensive "negative partisanship," Indian Americans played a pivotal role in delivering congressional majorities back to the Democratic Party. Here's what the data says.
What the numbers say: Story of 2026, 2024 and 2022
According to the pre-election survey conducted by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in partnership with YouGov, it was found that 62 per cent of Indian-American citizens intended to vote for Democratic congressional candidates, compared with 19 per cent for Republicans. Meanwhile, 12 per cent of the registered voters remained undecided.
The electoral trajectory of the Indian American diaspora over the last four years can be considered to resemble a political pendulum. Long considered one of the most reliably progressive voting blocs in the United States, the community showed major signs of fragmentation in 2024.
During the presidential race, Republican pick Donald Trump secured a historic 30 per cent of the Indian American vote. This hit the democrats hard, given that on the ballot opposite Trump was an Indian-American herself, Kamala Harris. While the majority, 62 per cent, still voted for Kamala, the surge in Trump's support in the community reflected how the Indian diaspora gave more weight to policy promises rather than the identity of the candidate.
In the 2022 midterms, 68 per cent of Indian-Americans voted Blue, while 29 per cent voted Republican. This year, the Carnegie noted that the population is voting for the Democrats because they have been upset with the policies of the Trump administration. The survey noted that 35 per cent of Indian Americans who voted for Democrats did so primarily out of opposition to the Republican Party and its policies rather than enthusiasm for the Democratic platform.
According to the data, one in four South Asian voters who supported Trump in 2024 switched sides to vote for Democratic congressional candidates. Not only that, but support for Republican House candidates plummeted to 19 per cent. Interestingly, the latest shift away from the Republicans was The shift away from the GOP was highly visible among older Indian American men (aged 40 and above). In January 2026, 32 per cent of this group supported Trump; by November 2026, their support for Republican midterm candidates dropped to just 16 per cent.
Pre-election data is not the only indicator of the shift. An election data analysis published by the Hindustan Times showed that the Democratic Party overwhelmingly swept congressional districts with large Indian American populations, winning 84 out of the 100 seats that feature the country's highest concentrations of Indian Americans. Hence, this dense geographic alignment directly fueled the broader Democratic recapture of majorities in both the US Senate and the House.
Reasons for the shift
So what triggered the realignment? The answer lies at the intersection of kitchen-table economics and immigration security.
While Indian Americans voted in 2024 hoping for inflation relief, the reality of Trump’s second-term immigration agenda sent shockwaves through the community. The administration’s implementation of a steep $100,000 filing fee on certain new H-1B visas, escalating threats to dismantle H-4 dependent work permits, and rigid bottlenecks in employment-based green card processing directly threatened the legal status and economic security of thousands of diaspora families.
While only Indian-American citizens vote in the polls, the visa crackdown impacts their relatives, contributing to their decision. Things became worse with a sharp rise in anti-immigrant and anti-Indian rhetoric originating from the Maga base.
In September 2026, the US Department of Homeland Security shared an image of a Transformers character confronting a Sikh man. The post carried the caption, "America for Americans. Get off our roads. You don't know how to drive, Mr Singh". The post was referring to a truck crash involving an Indian driver. It soon garnered severe backlash, prompting the DHS to delete the post.
Earlier this year, Bo French, a Republican candidate for Texas Railroad Commissioner, shared a photograph of University of Texas students celebrating a football victory and claimed it showed how many Americans had been "displaced by foreigners". The post garnered bipartisan backlash as well, following which French said that he was criticising immigration policies and not targeting any community.
French eventually lost the midterms to Democrats' Jon Rosenthal. Soon after his loss, Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi shared the tweet and wrote, "Bye Bye Bo. Bigotry is a losing strategy."
Lessons for 2028
The 2026 midterms have sent a definitive message to both political establishments.
For the Republicans, the results prove that economic outreach to legal immigrants cannot survive simultaneous policy crackdowns on high-skilled visas and alienating rhetoric.
For the Democrats, the victory comes with a warning: the diaspora has returned, but their loyalty is conditional. If Democrats want to hold this ground heading into the 2028 presidential cycle, they must address the core economic and immigration backlogs that made voters restless in the first place. The Indian diaspora votes on policies, not on identity politics.

news.title: Democrats Sweep Midterms but Face a Looming Civil War Over 2028
news.text:
A blue tsunami swept across the United States on Tuesday, November 3, as Democrats captured both the Senate and the House of Representatives in midterm elections. According to The New York Times, it was the party’s largest popular-vote victory since 1976 across all parties—a resounding triumph that appears to clear the road for the opposition to Donald Trump ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

Yet the sweeping success has also plunged the Democratic Party into a period of profound uncertainty, and potentially bitter conflict. With the notable exception of figures like the so-called “traitor” Haley Stevens in Michigan, centrists and progressives delivered victories for the party across the country, burying—at least halfway—the hatchet for the duration of the campaign.

But the truce may prove short-lived, as presidential ambitions on all sides have sharpened over the months. A wide gulf remains between moderates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Governor Gavin Newsom, and the party’s progressive stars like Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez—comfortably reelected in New York—and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The party’s left flank takes a more radical stance on economic issues such as taxes and healthcare access, as well as on social matters.

No Clear Winner Between the Party’s Wings

Those who hoped the midterms would settle the score between the two camps have reason to be disappointed. “Progressives or centrists”—”nearly every Democrat running in high-profile races won,” The Washington Post summarized on Thursday, noting that “few could claim their wing alone led the party to victory.”

That has not stopped some from arguing the results prove one faction’s dominance. “Democratic wins fuel the fight between centrists and progressives over the path forward to 2028,” The Hill headlined on Wednesday.

On the party’s left, lawmakers are celebrating the election of progressive representatives such as Claire Valdez in New York, along with several encouraging Senate results. Troy D. Jackson and Abdul El-Sayed won tightly contested and closely watched races in Maine and Michigan, while socialist Angie Nixon, defeated in Florida, still surprised observers by capturing 48 percent of the vote—more than polls had predicted.

That was enough for New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to declare that choosing a progressive candidate for 2028 is “absolutely” possible, if not necessary. The mayor, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, told NBC it is “crucial” that Democrats recognize “by examining their victories… the urgency of delivering change that Americans can feel in their wallets.”

“Listening to the left, what a concept!” Usamah Andrabi quipped in a Wednesday post on X. For the spokesperson of the progressive Justice Democrats caucus, speaking to The Guardian, the election confirmed popular support for “a bold and visionary agenda” on economic issues.

That could further whet the appetite of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a putative 2028 candidate. The New York progressive is “the big winner of the night,” one source told The Hill, arguing the midterms have boosted “populism” and shown she is “well positioned” for the White House.

Centrists Remain Deeply Entrenched

Evidence of the party’s ambiguity came in the form of a rather opposite diagnosis from The New York Times, which published a Wednesday article headlined around moderates who are “increasing their numbers and influence.” Less left-leaning Democrats “spent months persuading voters in Republican-leaning states or swing districts,” the newspaper argued, crediting them with “largely” charting the path to victory.

Reinforced ranks on the party’s right and center give House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and Senate counterpart Chuck Schumer hope of ultimately presiding over both chambers of Congress. Their hold on their leadership posts had seemed far from assured recently, given the criticism both moderates face from their left. The sweeping victory in both chambers could even weaken progressives, whose voices will carry less weight in securing majorities.

For 2028, several Democrats positioned closer to the center clearly distinguished themselves during the midterms, starting with Pastor James Talarico, whose landslide victory in Texas—a Republican stronghold—drew widespread commentary. While he has not expressed interest in the White House, “he won by 12 points, which is enormous and gives him a certain legitimacy,” Jérôme Viala-Gaudefroy, a doctor of American civilization, told Le HuffPost on Wednesday, the day after the vote.

The expert also pointed to Jon Ossoff, the senator overwhelmingly reelected in Georgia, whose name keeps surfacing in the media and whom many compare to a certain Barack Obama—who passed through the Senate before the White House. “He said he would stay in Congress for the six years of his term, but there will eventually be pressure to push him to run,” Viala-Gaudefroy analyzed.

Faced with the “major differences” between the party’s left and right wings, the expert believes the 2028 primaries will determine “which current truly wins.” History will tell whether the debates unify the party—or turn into a bloodbath just before the presidential election.

news.title: Editorial | CARICOM post-US midterm elections
news.text:
The shellacking of the Republican Party in the US midterm elections suggests that while it may have been badly stressed, America’s institutions didn’t collapse. The country’s democracy remained intact.

The questions still to be answered, however, are whether Tuesday’s vote was primarily a response by Americans to domestic economic concerns, or a fundamental repudiation of Trumpism and, therefore, its implications for the global environment.

While the mercurial Donald Trump still controls critical levers of power in the US government and may continue to lash out at perceived enemies, the potential for congressional checks on his worst instincts during the final two years of his presidency is cause for optimism, especially for small countries like Jamaica and its partners in the Caribbean. They may find some breathing space from the frenetic and febrile pressure from the Trump administration for uncritical obeisance to Washington.

In that regard, the 14 independent members of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) should urgently convene a special summit to coordinate how they navigate the final years of Mr Trump’s term. Failing to do so before Mr Trump’s assumption of office meant they largely had to scramble separately to deflect the whimsy and extremism of the president’s policymaking. The result in many cases was meek acquiescence.

 FAR-RIGHT 

After more than a decade of Mr Trump’s dominance of the Republican Party – which he essentially transformed into a far-right, largely ethnocentric movement that, with little regard for small countries or a rules-based global order – the scale of his and the party’s defeat this week was monumental. The Democratic Party beat the Republicans in the congressional races by an estimated 13 percentage points for a swing, compared to the 2024 midterms, of 15.6 percentage points.

Only in the 2010 elections, at the height of the Tea Party movement, did rampaging congressional Republicans achieve a swing of 17.3 percentage points. However, you have to go back to the post-Watergate period, after Richard Nixon’s resignation in 1974, for a margin of victory (16.8 percentage points) at this level, or surpassing, what the Democrats accomplished this week. They are assured of at least 250 House seats and 54 in the Senate, giving them majorities in both chambers.

Democrats won among all demographic groups: seven in 10 among people aged 18 to 29; six in 10 among Hispanics, nearly half of whose votes Mr Trump gained in 2024; nine in 10 of Black voters, against eight in 10 who supported Kamala Harris for president in 2024; voters of all educational levels, except for high school graduates, who almost evenly split, voted strongly for Democrats. Even among rural voters, the Democrats made significant headway, moving their support from 29 per cent in 2024 to 41 per cent on Tuesday.

Even in states where Republican support was deeply and historically entrenched, Democrats flipped seats. For example, Kansas is sending a Democrat to the Senate for the first time in 94 years. And before this week, the last time Texas elected a Democrat as either senator or governor was in 1988 and 1990, respectively.

Indeed, the outgoing governor of Florida called the defeat of members of his party, up and down the ballot across the country, “a close to extinction level event for Republicans”.

What is not clear as yet is what motivated this revolt by voters, apart from oil-price-driven inflation from the US/Israeli war on Iraq, and to a lesser extent, Mr Trump’s unilateral imposition of higher tariffs on imports from countries across the globe. A muscular immigration policy in which supposedly undocumented workers were often forcefully scooped up, denied due process and shunted out of the country, has also caused anxieties among voters.

 DEEP CONCERNS 

For most Caribbean countries there are deep concerns about Mr Trump’s reiteration of the Monroe Doctrine of US hegemony in the Western Hemisphere, and Washington’s pressure to sideline relations with China, which, in recent decades, has been their primary source of cheap capital for infrastructure projects. The US administration has also leaned on Caribbean countries, including Jamaica, to end health service agreements with Cuba, while it has intensified its economic blockade of Havana.

It is partly because of this pressure that Jamaica controversially abstained from an annual UN resolution calling on the United States to end its economic embargo on Cuba, and why it is believed Kingston didn’t vote on a resolution to accept the annual report from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which the Trump administration wants to dismantle.

Claiming them to be illegal combatants engaged in war against the United States, Mr Trump has used its military to blow up alleged drug-smuggling vessels in the Caribbean Sea, which experts not only say breaches domestic and international law, but undermines the declaration of the Caribbean as a zone of peace.

If the electoral chastening of Mr Trump causes a cooling of this behaviour, it will be good for the Caribbean. CARICOM should not be passive on the matter. It must consider how it deals with the White House while engaging with the Democrats who now control Congress.

news.title: Who’s Left?
news.text:
Republicans and pundits will play the “blame game” for a while and try to analyze “what happened” on Tuesday, November 3. And perhaps we can learn something (I doubt it). But I’m not going to do that in this article (although I just did it in a video podcast on my Substack). Tuesday’s done; it’s over, and we can’t change the results. We can try to learn from it (again, we probably won’t), pick up the pieces, and try to make sure it never happens again. And, well, it’s not like it’s never happened before. The Republicans lost 41 seats in the House in 2018, though, interestingly, they actually gained two seats in the Senate. 2026, obviously, is much worse.

So, pick up the pieces. What’s left? Frankly, not much. I’m not sure Texas is totally gone, like California and New York are, but if so, that would be very damaging. Florida is now the main Republican bulwark. What else? Well, Alabama, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma are still pretty solid (Mississippi not so much so; Georgia is gone); Tennessee and West Virginia are still strongly Republican (I have worries about Kentucky’s inconsistency), and then there are Wyoming, Idaho, and Utah that are very dependable, with maybe Montana and the Dakotas. Indiana can usually be counted on, and Missouri, too.

And that’s just about it. Republicans have about 10 “solids” and a few “usuallys.” Fifteen or so out of 50. Alaska and Mississippi may go for Democratic senators this year (it’s still undecided at this writing), but any state that repeatedly elects Lisa Murkowski as senator (Alaska) isn’t to be trusted anyway. There’s just not much left, folks, and except for Florida, the populations of all the rest of those states combined aren’t much more than California’s. Only Tennessee ranks in the top 15 in state population. In fact, let me list the top 15 states in population:

1. California: 39,355,309

2. Texas: 31,709,821

3. Florida: 23,462,518

4. New York: 20,002,427

5. Pennsylvania: 13,059,432

6. Illinois: 12,719,141

7. Ohio: 11,900,510

8. Georgia: 11,302,748

9. North Carolina: 11,197,968

10. Michigan: 10,127,884

11. New Jersey: 9,548,215

12. Virginia: 8,880,107

13. Washington: 8,001,020

14. Arizona: 7,623,818

15. Tennessee: 7,315,076

That is not a long list of states that voted Republican this year, or generally do so, and pardon my sarcasm. Yes, Mr. Trump won several of them in 2016 and 2024, but we mustn’t overlook who Trump defeated — Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. If you can find me two more…unattractive, unappealing, unpleasant, distasteful women in the United States than those two, I’d like to know who they are (they do have some competition, I admit). So, did the American people really find Donald Trump so overwhelmingly appealing that they gave him victories, or was he greatly assisted by Democratic Party stupidity?

Well, be that as it may, my point here is that only two of the top 15 states in population are reliably Republican, and one of those is number 15. And of the Western states that are “reliably” Republican, only Utah has a population over three million. Many Democratic hellhole urban areas have more people than most of the western states. Demographics are not with the Republicans here, not for the foreseeable future.

And even when the Republicans win the House of Representatives now, they get the barest of majorities and a weak Speaker. Democrats are going to have well over 250 seats in the House this term with a belligerent Speaker who hates Republicans and America. The Republicans did have 53 Senate seats the past two years; the Democrats will have at least 54 this time (two are still undecided, and right now the votes are being led by Democrats). And, of course, add several RINOs to the Democratic number. There are no “DINOs” on the Democratic Party side of the aisle. It’s not pretty.

I’m not trying to be pessimistic here; I’m just trying to be realistic. We don’t have many reliable states left, while the Democrats have many they can always count on, and those are most of the largest states in the Union. Republicans need to be trying to build some new coalitions, but…who? Unfortunately, America is moving leftward toward dependence and decadence, and those two qualities are tailor-made for Democrats.

Righteous nations do not fall; the people in such a country have the qualities and characteristics necessary to remain spiritually, morally, and nationally strong. While never perfect, America became a great nation because its people were largely spiritually and morally united. When decadence sets in, a nation begins to decline and ultimately collapse. And it’s happening rapidly in America now.

America, today, can in no shape, form, or fashion be called a “righteous” nation anymore. There are still good, godly people in the country, of course, but they are far in the minority now. No nation that lets its babies be murdered in the womb, that butchers its children for sexual purposes, that exalts sexual immorality and perversion, that doesn’t know the difference between a man and a woman, or what marriage and a family are anymore, that opens its borders and lets criminals walk the streets with impunity…no nation that allows and tolerates those things, much less has its majority political party supporting them, can be called “righteous.” Decadent, yes. Righteous, no.

When God is removed from the human spirit, the only thing that remains is an animal and a jungle. Like what America has become in too many places now, and like America elected in so many places on Tuesday. The dominance of evil human hearts is the supreme problem America now faces — in the streets and in government — and that is a problem that is exceedingly difficult to solve. How do you change the human heart?

So, after Tuesday, who’s left? Not very many, I’m afraid. But that doesn’t mean we quit fighting; it only means we fight harder.

news.title: How A Viral Ad And Trump Rally Appearance Put A Democrat In The Spotlight
news.text: A viral campaign ad and an unexpected appearance at a Donald Trump rally have helped Democratic candidate Scott Colom turn a difficult Senate campaign into a surprisingly close contest in Mississippi.Colom, who was considered a long-shot candidate, has taken a lead of more than 1,700 votes over Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. With more than 95 per cent of the votes counted, the race remains too close to call.Mississippi is traditionally a Republican stronghold. Trump won the state by around 23 percentage points in 2024, and it has not elected a Democrat to the US Senate in more than 40 years.According to The New York Times, a major turning point came in October when a short campaign ad by Colom went viral. The video highlighted Hyde-Smith's response to a local television anchor's question about rising beef prices. She suggested that people had other sources of protein to choose from.The advert then showed a man grilling burgers, who responded that he would rather choose another senator. The message connected with voters concerned about rising food prices and gave Colom's campaign fresh attention.The advert also attracted national Democratic support. The Senate Majority PAC invested $2.2 million in the race, while the Democratic Senate campaign organisation contributed another $500,000. Former President Barack Obama recorded an endorsement advert, while Bill Clinton, Kamala Harris and several Democratic senators campaigned for Colom.An unusual appearance at Trump's rallyColom also made headlines by attending Trump's rally in support of Hyde-Smith. Rather than avoiding the event, he spoke to people waiting outside, listening to their concerns about healthcare, grocery bills and fuel prices.The New York Times reported that Colom also took selfies with rally-goers and later said he had won over some Republican voters.In an interview with CNN, he promised to work towards lower grocery prices, an end to wars and the full release of the Epstein files.Colom also received strong support from Black voters, who make up around 37 per cent of Mississippi's population. He performed particularly well in predominantly Black counties.However, the final result could take several more days. Counties can accept certain mailed and provisional ballots until next Tuesday, with certified results due to the state by 13 November.Mississippi does not have a standard recount process for statewide general elections. The final result is expected to be certified by 3 December.The unexpectedly close race has put national attention on Mississippi and turned Colom into one of the most talked-about Democratic candidates in the country.
news.summary: A viral campaign advert and an unexpected appearance at Donald Trump's rally have helped Democrat Scott Colom challenge Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi.

news.title: Thumbs down for Donald Trump
news.text:
In the United States, midterm elections are almost always bad for the president’s party, so it was taken for granted that this time round Republican candidates would have a hard time of it. But few imagined that even in Texas, of all places, they would get clobbered by their Democrat rivals. Of course, the big loser was Donald Trump. Though he reacted immediately to the massacre by pointing out that his name was not on the ballot, until that moment he had been doing his energetic best to persuade voters that the legislative elections, like everything else that happens in the universe, were all about him. Large numbers took him at his word.

Even among those who on the whole greatly prefer Trump’s overall approach to his country’s worst problems to that of any Democrat faction, there are many who think he thoroughly deserved the shellacking he received. As well as being put off by his increasingly obnoxious behaviour, they have come to suspect that, in his 80s, he is simply losing it. Some compare him to “sleepy Joe” Biden in the months preceding the elections of 2024 when the then president hoping to get re-elected had to give way to the word-salad expert Kamala Harris.

Hours before voters made their way to the polling booths, Trump spent about 20 minutes droning on in a public speech about the beauties of the reflecting pool he had built beside the Lincoln Memorial. It would have been difficult for him to come up with a better way of telling his compatriots that he was completely out of touch with their concerns and was determined to remain so.

After the votes were counted, pundits of all kinds agreed that the Republicans – that is Trump – lost badly because the government has failed to deliver on the bread-and-butter issues that are summed up in the voguish word “affordability.” Much the same problem had made life difficult for the Democrats two years earlier. It would seem that, throughout the West, most people take it for granted that politicians should be able to improve the living standards of ordinary folk but refuse to do so for sinister reasons. Unfortunately, things are rather more complicated. Economies everywhere are evolving in such a way that, while a fairly large minority is doing very well, those further down the food chain are losing ground, a tendency that seems certain to intensify in the coming months and years after getting turbocharged by Artificial Intelligence.

Trump, and the Republican Party, got to where they are by cleverly taking advantage of the disgruntlement of the millions of people who felt that, in addition to falling behind economically, they were being subjected to a bizarre experiment by cultish “woke” fanatics seeking to indoctrinate them. news.title: Voters are turning out in droves to cut autocrats down to size
news.text:
It’s not just the US midterms: An anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world.
In country after country that has struggled with creeping authoritarianism and democratic decay, outraged electorates have turned out in record numbers, delivering indisputable victories that have checked the autocratic advance.
The United States crossed into “competitive authoritarianism” during President Donald Trump’s second term, according to eminent political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan A. Way. Voters issued a stunning rebuke in the midterms, when an expected blue wave turned out to be a blue tsunami.
The outpouring was just what Kamala Harris, the former Democratic presidential contender, urged before the vote when she told supporters, “We just need to turn out in really large numbers that would be too big to rig.” It even overcame exceptional efforts by Trump and his party to gerrymander impenetrable Republican districts.
Voters are still seen as more likely to go to the polls to defend their pocketbooks than democratic principles. But when those issues intersect – for instance, in angry accusations of corruption, at a time when voters are struggling economically – the combination has proved especially motivating.
The year has provided a host of examples, as voters turned out in numbers that capsized the efforts of nationalist autocrats, tainted by corruption accusations, to tilt the political playing field their way even before elections could begin.
Last month, when Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s longtime nationalist strongman, was swept out of power, estimates suggested that voter turnout was nearly 70%, the highest since the breakup of the former Yugoslavia.
In Brazil, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was jailed for attempting a coup after he lost the last election to Lula. In this year’s election, turnout increased by nearly 3 million voters between the first and second rounds, bucking the usual trend of votes falling in the runoff. Voter absenteeism fell to the lowest level of any Brazilian presidential election.
In Hungary, Viktor Orban, a MAGA favorite who had proclaimed himself the champion of “illiberal democracy,” was ousted in April after nearly 16 successive years as prime minister. Voter turnout reached its highest level since the fall of Communism in 1989 – about 80%.
‘Too big to rig’
The overwhelming turnout and high margins of those victories were important, because they neutralized the tactics that authoritarian leaders often use to prejudice electoral outcomes in their favor, said Kim L. Scheppele, a professor at Princeton University who studies democracy in Eastern Europe.
“If you have a close vote, then autocratic capture can always pull them over the line with dirty tricks of different kinds,” she said. But when the margin is huge, such tricks no longer work, and disfavored leaders must either step down or fully abandon democracy in favor of a violent crackdown, as former President Nicolás Maduro of Venezuela did when he faced a loss in 2024.
In Hungary, for example, the opposition Tisza party won an absolute majority in Parliament, overcoming even the rejigged rules that Orban had long used to ensure that a plurality of votes gave his party a supermajority in the legislature.
In Israel, by contrast, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in elections in October, due in part to record-high turnout among Israeli Arabs. But the coalition bargaining is so narrow that Netanyahu has tried to cast doubt on the results by claiming without evidence that the Arab parties stole the election.
Youth in revolt
Young people have been a crucial element of this new anti-authoritarian wave.
“I want to thank the generosity of Brazilian youth, who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech, referring to student protests that broke out after he finished in second place in the first round of the presidential election. In the second round, Lula’s substantial advantage with voters younger than 35 powered him to victory.
In the United States, 70% of all voters younger than 30 cast their ballots for Democrats, according to New York Times data. Even more notably, 61% of young men voted Democrat – a big change from 2024, when more than 56% of them supported Trump.
In Hungary, according to exit polls, 67% of voters younger than 30 cast their ballots for the victorious Tisza party, compared with just 8% for Orban’s party, Fidesz.
The most notable youth effects came in Serbia, where the opposition’s victory was driven by a new youth-led political bloc called Student List-Students Win, which grew out of a longtime student protest movement. The students recruited candidates from outside the political system: doctors, scientists and others. Their message – anti-politics but pro-democracy – resonated with voters.
“If you can get all new faces, then you can build these big-tent parties and let young people power it with social media,” Scheppele said. “Then you can get these huge election victories, which enable you to really root out the prior autocratic government.”
This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

news.title: ‘Thank you, LA’: Nithya Raman vows to build ‘extraordinary’ future after mayoral win
news.text:
Nithya Raman, who defeated incumbent Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, has thanked residents for their support and pledged to build a better future for the city, describing her election victory as a great honour.
Raman's victory comes amid a strong showing by Indian-American politicians in the November 3 US midterm elections, with several candidates winning congressional and state-level races.
In her first statement after the victory, Raman took to X to express gratitude to voters and acknowledge her predecessor's contribution to the city.
Los Angeles, I am deeply honored to be your next mayor.
I just spoke with Mayor Bass and expressed my deepest gratitude for her leadership and decades of service. Los Angeles would not be the city it is today without her.
I love this city. I believe in its people. The work ahead will be hard, and change will take time. And together, we are going to build a future as extraordinary as the city we call home.
Thank you, LA. Let’s get to work.
— Nithya Raman (@nithyavraman) November 5, 2026
"Los Angeles, I am deeply honored to be your next mayor. I just spoke with Mayor Bass and expressed my deepest gratitude for her leadership and decades of service. Los Angeles would not be the city it is today without her," she wrote.
"I love this city. I believe in its people. The work ahead will be hard, and change will take time. And together, we are going to build a future as extraordinary as the city we call home. Thank you, LA. Let's get to work," she added.
The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with the progressive Los Angeles City Council member securing 52 per cent of the vote. Bass subsequently conceded defeat.
With her victory, Raman has become the first Indian-American and South Asian mayor of Los Angeles, the second-largest city in the United States.
Her win also means that two of the country's largest cities are now led by mayors of Indian descent. The other is New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who took office in January 2026.
Raman defeated Bass despite the incumbent receiving support from prominent Democrats, including California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice-President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.
Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), marking another significant electoral victory for the progressive political movement.
From Kerala to Harvard and MIT
Born in Kerala in 1981, Raman moved to the United States with her family when she was six. She studied at Harvard University before earning a master's degree in urban planning from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT).
After completing her education, she returned to India and worked on urban development initiatives, particularly projects aimed at improving living conditions for marginalised communities.
She moved to Los Angeles in 2013, where she worked with the city's administration and became involved in efforts to address homelessness. She also helped establish the SELAH Neighborhood Homeless Coalition in 2017.
Raman entered electoral politics in 2020, defeating incumbent David Ryu to represent Los Angeles's fourth council district. She was re-elected in 2024.
Her mayoral campaign took an unexpected turn after she withdrew her initial support for Bass's re-election bid and entered the race in February, just hours before the filing deadline, Al Jazeera reported.
Housing, homelessness at the centre of campaign
Raman campaigned on changing what she described as Los Angeles's "broken status quo", promising to address the city's longstanding problems.
In her victory speech, she pledged to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.
"For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do," she told supporters.
Her key promises included expanding affordable housing, tackling homelessness, improving neglected public services and repairing roads and infrastructure.
She also proposed deploying more medical teams to assist people experiencing homelessness and called for a different approach to the city's housing crisis.
Raman further pledged to protect residents from immigration enforcement efforts, safeguard Hollywood jobs amid industry cuts and improve neighbourhood facilities.
Her victory comes at a challenging time for Los Angeles, which continues to deal with a homelessness crisis, infrastructure concerns and the aftermath of the devastating January 2025 wildfires.
She will also have to prepare the city for the 2028 Olympic Games, which will bring additional demands on its infrastructure and public services, Aljazeera reported.
In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and said she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.
Thank you, Los Angeles. Serving as your mayor has been the honor of my life. https://t.co/ObC2zrVao9
— Karen Bass (@KarenBassLA) November 5, 2026
“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me. She added, moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us," Bass wrote.

news.title: Gavin Newsom Messed Up
news.text:
The midterms are over, and eyes are turning to the 2028 presidential race. Gavin Newsom — who led the betting odds to be the next Democratic presidential nominee from Donald Trump’s 2024 election until August of this year — had imagined that this would be his moment. 

Alas, right now, everyone is turning their attention to younger candidates, such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. In the case of Ossoff, he feels like a breath of fresh air to Democrats in comparison to Newsom and his scandals. Ossoff’s first and only wife is a beautiful doctor, and he has two young daughters. He is politically talented and only 39 years old. (RELATED: 2028 Begins!)

Newsom, on the other hand, has a list of scandals that leaves a bad taste in Democrats’ mouths, all of which I chronicle in my book, Newsom Unleashed: The Progressive Lust for Unbridled Power.

He was married to Kimberly Guilfoyle, who is now the face of alleged MAGA corruption. He had an affair with a young mother, Ruby Rippey, who was in the throes of addiction to cocaine. (Recently, she revealed in Vanity Fair that she was blackout drunk during some of their sexual encounters.) He dated a teenager while mayor of San Francisco. He has admitted to being at his mother’s bedside when she was illegally euthanized. He holds responsibility for California’s homelessness epidemic, as well as numerous other crises in California, from the highest cost of living in the nation to the highest unemployment rate in the nation. (READ MORE: Newsom’s Affair Partner Reveals She Was Blackout Drunk During Encounters)

There’s so much more. He rose up in San Francisco politics as the playboy adopted son of Gordon Getty, and his companies were bankrolled into existence by Getty. He had problems with alcohol as mayor. He aroused national hatred for dining at the French Laundry while telling his citizens to wear masks between bites of food. (RELATED: Gavin Newsom’s Pandemic Regrets Tour) 

There’s more. Newsom was the No. 1 defender of the cognitively addled Joe Biden. Even after the disastrous debate in which Biden revealed he had lost it, Newsom decided to travel around the country to convince Democrats to stick with Biden. (RELATED: Gavin Newsom Breaks With Biden to Set Up Presidential Run)

Newsom’s former chief of staff — who served in that office from 2023 to 2024 — has pleaded guilty to three federal charges related to schemes she was part of while she occupied that office, and she has stated that the feds under Joe Biden tried to get her to implicate Newsom in wrongdoing.

And now, Newsom and his wife are under federal investigation. That investigation is drawing headlines and attention, as recent news reports reveal that some of the investigation centers on the funding of his international travel. Newsom claims it’s all an effort by Trump to prevent him from seeking the White House, but Department of Justice sources have assured media outlets that the investigation is very much legitimate and serious. (READ MORE: The Feds Are Closing In on Newsom — and His Corporate Bankrollers)

Why on earth would Democrats go with this man? At some point, all of this is just too unpleasant for donors and voters to swallow.

I realized Newsom had messed up when he launched his memoir in February of this year and embarked on a major media tour to sell it. There was a Vogue puff piece, a New York Times profile, and a nearly 4,000-word New Yorker profile. He was starting his campaign way too soon. His plan had been to try to get his scandals dealt with and out of the way before the election began, but the end result is that he seems stale and like last year’s news. 

When his book came out, I said, “But this is all way too early. The public only has so much appetite for following any candidate’s moment in the spotlight. If Newsom tries to manufacture another moment for himself a year from now, Americans will be too bored to pay attention.”

“He’s wasting political capital when few Americans care,” I said. “And worst of all, as the frontrunner, he’s painting a giant target on his back and inviting fellow Democratic hopefuls to shoot.” (READ MORE: Gavin Newsom Will Regret His Book Launch)

Democrats have also gotten annoyed with Newsom’s obsession with himself, seeing in it echoes of Trump’s own egomania. In January of this year, David Axelrod complained publicly about Newsom’s “self-puffery.”

Newsom was leading in the betting odds to be the next Democratic nominee until he was passed by Ocasio-Cortez in mid-August, according to Kalshi. Right after the midterm elections, Jon Ossoff garnered significant hype and jumped to a 26.3 percent chance of winning the nomination. Newsom, meanwhile, fell to being tied with Ocasio-Cortez at a 13.6 percent chance of winning the nomination. Meanwhile, the New York Times average of the 15 most recent polls on the Democratic primary race puts former Vice President Kamala Harris in first place with 34 percent support and Newsom in second place with 20 percent support. He is followed by Pete Buttigieg, Ocasio-Cortez, and Ossoff.

News reports are now beginning to say that some Democrats have soured on Newsom.

Page Six published an article Thursday claiming, via anonymous sources, that Democratic insiders say donors “may have tired” of Newsom.

The source said, “He seems to have peaked too early.” According to Page Six’s account, this is because people are talking more about Newsom’s affair with Ruby Rippey and the federal investigation into him and his wife than his presidential campaign.

“All of a sudden, Gavin Newsom with all his drama doesn’t seem as appealing as Beshear or Ossoff,” the person said.

Meanwhile, a different source told Page Six: “The media loves him because he’s good copy. But I am amazed how the donor orbit is over him. His moment is in the past. There’s baggage and then there’s Titanic steamer trunks of baggage. Let’s not forget he was married to Kimberly Guilfoyle, and the state of California is such a mess.”

Indeed, last month I wrote that Newsom would likely have to spend his entire campaign explaining why he married the woman who is “a living caricature of a corrupt, morally bankrupt MAGA woman” in the eyes of Democrats. (READ MORE: Gavin Newsom’s Awkward Marriage to Kimberly Guilfoyle) 

But never underestimate Gavin Newsom’s ability to rise from the ashes after a horrible scandal. There’s been scandal after scandal in his nearly 30 years in public office, and he is still at the top of the national conversation.

Donald Trump is an instructive case that voters can look past personal baggage, improprieties, and political scandals, and that these can, in fact, give interest to a candidate. Trump is also a case study in how prosecutions pursued under the leadership of the opposite party can backfire. Trump’s second term in office is, after all, a direct result of the prosecution by New York District Attorney Alvin Bragg.

Newsom is still a darling of the Left. For example, Vanity Fair’s October edition features a thousands-of-words-long profile of the California governor and his preparations to pursue the presidency. He has a huge base of donors behind him, and he has made himself out to be the Democrats’ top opponent against Trump. He has been preparing for this moment all his life.

Never underestimate Newsom’s ability to rise from the ashes, but, at some point, Democrats must get sick of him.

Ellie Gardey Holmes is the author of Newsom Unleashed: The Progressive Lust for Unbridled Power.

news.title: Who is Harmeet Dhillon? The Indian-origin lawyer exiting Trump's administration after a rocky tenure
news.text:
Harmeet Kaur Dhillon, an Indian-origin Republican lawyer who led the US Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, has resigned from her position and plans to return to the private legal sector.
Dhillon stepped down on November 5, ending her tenure as Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights. She was nominated by US President Donald Trump in December 2024 and confirmed by the Senate in April 2025.
Her resignation comes amid a major political shift in Washington following the 2026 midterm elections, in which Democrats secured control of both chambers of Congress.
Dhillon is a prominent conservative lawyer and political activist who has spent years representing Republican politicians, campaigns and organisations in legal disputes involving free speech, civil liberties and constitutional rights.
Serving my country as AAG for Civil Rights has been the honor of a lifetime. We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more. I want to thank President Trump for giving me this opportunity. I look forward to what’s next!
— AAGHarmeetDhillon (@AAGDhillon) November 5, 2026
Who is Harmeet Dhillon?
Born in Chandigarh, India, Dhillon moved to the United States with her family at a young age. She grew up in New York and North Carolina before pursuing a career in law.
She graduated from Dartmouth College with a degree in Classical Studies before earning her Juris Doctor from the University of Virginia School of Law in 1993. During her time there, she served on the editorial board of the Virginia Law Review.
After graduating, Dhillon clerked for Judge Paul V. Niemeyer of the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit. She subsequently worked at several corporate law firms before establishing her own practice, Dhillon Law Group Inc., in San Francisco in 2006.
Her firm handles commercial litigation, free speech disputes, political law and civil liberties cases.
In 2018, she also founded the Center for American Liberty, a conservative nonprofit legal organisation focused on civil rights litigation.
How Dhillon became a prominent Republican figure
Dhillon gradually built a strong presence in Republican politics, holding several leadership positions within the party.
She served as chair of the San Francisco Republican Party and vice chair of the California Republican Party. She also represented California as a Republican National Committeewoman from 2016 to 2025.
Her legal practice brought her into contact with prominent conservative politicians, political campaigns and public figures, representing clients in disputes involving constitutional rights, media and free speech.
In January 2023, Dhillon made a bid for the chairmanship of the Republican National Committee (RNC), challenging incumbent Ronna McDaniel.
Although she did not win the position, the contest raised her national profile within the Republican Party.
Dhillon's role in the US Justice Department
Trump nominated Dhillon to lead the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division in December 2024. The US Senate confirmed her appointment in April 2025 by a 52-45 vote.
She became the first Republican woman and the first Republican of Indian origin to head the division.
The Civil Rights Division is responsible for enforcing federal laws protecting people against discrimination in areas including employment, housing, education, voting and access to public services.
A controversial past, a turbulent tenure
Dhillon has rarely been far from controversy, facing political and legal scrutiny at several stages of her career.
Before joining the government, she drew criticism from fellow Republicans over her past association with the ACLU and political donations to Democrats, including Kamala Harris. Her 2023 campaign for RNC chair was also reportedly dogged by a whisper campaign targeting her Sikh faith. Meanwhile, her law firm represented prominent conservative clients in contentious cases, including legal challenges to the 2020 US election results.
But her time as Assistant Attorney General for the Civil Rights Division from 2025 to 2026 brought the sharpest scrutiny. Dhillon reshaped the division's priorities, directing its resources towards issues favoured by conservatives, including corporate diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) programmes, municipal gender policies and access to state voter registration data. The changes triggered fierce criticism and deep internal turmoil, with more than 75 per cent of the division's career legal staff reportedly leaving during her tenure.

news.title: Trailing MAGA Republican begs for recount cash: ‘Costs money every single hour’
news.text:
Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith's (R-MS) campaign is appealing to donors to cover legal costs as she trails Democrat Scott Colom in Mississippi’s Senate race, Politico reported on Thursday.

Mississippi and Alaska are the last two uncalled Senate races, Politico reported, and both parties are raising money for possible recounts, although control of the Senate is already settled. Hyde-Smith is behind Colom by under 2,000 votes with over 95 percent of ballots in. In Alaska, Sen. Dan Sullivan trails Democrat Mary Peltola by a little over 600 votes with roughly three-quarters counted.

Both these results in red states would be political earthquakes if they hold.

A Thursday email from Hyde-Smith’s campaign said legal fights across the state demand major resources and that having lawyers monitor ballots and defend the seat “costs money every single hour,” according to Politico. The Senate Republicans’ campaign arm set up a recount fund on Election Day, adding Sullivan first and Hyde-Smith by Wednesday morning.

Democrats are fundraising as well. Colom’s campaign launched a legal fund, and Politico reviewed emails on his behalf sent to the lists of the Democratic National Committee, Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Gov. Wes Moore (D-MD), Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-GA), and others.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris sent her own appeal, writing that Republicans “will not let another go without a fight.”

Politico says what happens next is unclear. Alaska counts slowly and uses ranked-choice voting, so if neither Sullivan nor Peltola reaches 50 percent in the first round, tabulation is expected in mid-November. Mississippi has no legal provision for a recount, automatic or requested, so court action would likely come first.

The Trump administration tried to sue Alaska before the election over the presence of another candidate with the same name as Sullivan, but this suit was dismissed.

news.title: Who Is Nithya Raman? India-Born Democratic Socialist Who Defeated Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass
news.text:
India-born Nithya Raman, a relatively little-known Los Angeles City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass in a stunning electoral upset, setting the stage for a significant political shift in the country's second-largest city.
Raman's victory represents a generational change in Los Angeles politics, following a similar trend in New York, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor last year. However, unlike Mamdani, Raman did not attract widespread national attention during her campaign and sought to establish herself as a candidate willing to differ with her own progressive political camp on certain issues.
The 45-year-old urban planner entered the mayoral contest after a dramatic reversal, having initially backed Bass, who was once her political ally. Raman eventually announced her own candidacy shortly before the filing deadline, arguing that the city had reached a "breaking point".
Bass' defeat makes her the first Los Angeles mayor in 20 years to lose a re-election bid. Her tenure was significantly affected by the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was overseas and caught the city's fire department unprepared. The destruction and its aftermath left many residents holding the mayor accountable, dealing a blow to her chances of securing another term.
Raman Promises Changes In Policing, Basic Civic Services
Raman's rise comes amid growing divisions within the Democratic Party, with left-wing challengers increasingly taking on establishment candidates across the country.
Among her key campaign promises is the removal of Los Angeles Police Chief, whom she considers too accommodating towards federal immigration authorities. She has also pledged to address the deterioration of essential civic services, with residents grappling with pothole-filled roads, damaged sidewalks, unclean neighbourhoods and non-functional streetlights.
Raman was also critical of Bass' handling of homelessness, describing the incumbent's efforts as ineffective. She has proposed a different approach that would involve expanding medical teams working with people living in homeless encampments and on the streets. The aim, according to her plan, is to establish trust with homeless residents and eventually help them move indoors.
Her proposals also include increasing the availability of housing to relocate people currently accommodated in hotels rented by the city as part of its homelessness response.
Raman has said her strategy could bring down the number of people sleeping in tents and encampments by at least half by 2028, when Los Angeles is scheduled to host the Olympic Games. However, homelessness has remained a persistent challenge in the region despite billions of dollars being spent to address the crisis.
Homelessness, Public Safety Among Voters' Top Concerns
Raman's campaign gained momentum amid voter dissatisfaction over problems that have continued to affect Los Angeles during Bass' tenure. Bass, 73, faced a challenger who positioned herself as the candidate of change in a city struggling with longstanding civic issues.
A Berkeley IGS/LA Times poll conducted between October 19 and 25 found that approximately four in 10 likely voters wanted reducing homeless encampments to be a top priority for the next mayor. Around three in 10 identified public safety or the construction of more affordable housing as key concerns.
Raman also managed to counter Bass' criticism that she was "not ready for primetime" and lacked the experience required to govern a city with a population of 3.8 million.
Her campaign focused heavily on the city's unresolved problems and questioned Bass' leadership. In one advertisement, Raman highlighted several troubled locations, including the site of a massive warehouse fire last summer, the homeless hub of Skid Row and shuttered shopping centres and storefronts.
"Our city is in crisis," she said in the advertisement, which showed an empty lectern. "Where is our mayor?" Raman asked.
Bass, meanwhile, maintained that her administration had made sufficient progress to deserve another four-year term. She also attempted to portray Raman's positions on policing and homelessness as "extreme".
Raman Wins Despite Limited Support From Democratic Establishment
Raman's victory came despite receiving considerably less backing from prominent Democratic leaders than her rival. Bass enjoyed the support of California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Almost every member of the Los Angeles City Council also backed her campaign.
Before becoming mayor in 2022, Bass had served in California's state Legislature and the US Congress. She had also been considered as a potential running mate for former President Joe Biden in the 2020 presidential election.
Billionaire real estate developer Rick Caruso, who lost to Bass in the 2022 mayoral contest, also signalled his preference for the incumbent this time. Although he did not formally endorse her, Caruso publicly said he would vote for Bass, an important indication of support from the business community.
Raman, on the other hand, secured backing from several advocacy and political organisations, including Our Revolution, established by Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and the Sierra Club. However, her campaign had relatively few endorsements from influential local politicians.
She also held a widely publicised private meeting with former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger, who did not take an active role in the mayoral contest. The meeting indicated Raman's efforts to widen her political network beyond her existing support base.
Building a broader circle of political and business allies could prove important as Raman prepares to govern a city with diverse economic interests. Los Angeles is home to a major port, leading universities and research institutions, a prominent entertainment industry and a substantial tourism sector, all of which present distinct challenges for its incoming administration.
