news.title: FREDDY GRAY: From the trans activist elected in Alabama to the hard-Left New Yorker who wants a world without borders... just wait until the Americans sick of Trump realise who they've sent to Washington!
news.text:
On Tuesday, something astonishing happened in the city of Huntsville, Alabama: voters elected as their state representative a transgender Democrat called Allison Montgomery.

The software engineer, who used to be called William, campaigned against legal sex-based definitions and the right of parents to know if their child is ‘transitioning’.

Montgomery is not, in other words, the sort of candidate you’d expect to win in ‘Bama’ – sweet home of the conservative South.

But it happened. And the main reason for that is not that the residents of Huntsville, the site of a major army base, have all suddenly turned ultra-woke.

It’s that the people of Alabama, who voted for Donald Trump three times, are now so furious with the President and his party that they are willing to elect just about anyone else. So are voters in Texas, Kansas, and North Carolina – three other ‘deep-red states’ that are now turning Democratic blue. The Maga electorate is livid about the failed Iran war, the spike in gas and food prices, and the brazen corruption of Trump’s Washington.

But that doesn’t mean all America has suddenly fallen in love with the Democrats. On the contrary, numerous polls suggest that, if anything, the Democratic ‘brand’ remains almost as toxic as it was two years ago, when Trump routed Kamala Harris to win the White House.

But, as even the President himself said on Wednesday, ‘the Democrats did a good job’ in the midterms.

What he meant was that his opponents successfully hid their more unpopular positions from the electorate, while staying laser-focused on the cost of living, what they call the billionaire ‘oligarchy’, and Team Trump’s many glaring faults.

After the failure of Joe Biden and his successor candidate in 2024, Harris, Democratic campaign organisations sent out repeated ‘message discipline’ memos to their candidates urging them to ditch the ultra-progressive rhetoric on gender pronouns and so on.

The candidates took note. In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, who will now be America’s first Muslim senator, went on Fox News, where he batted away questions about his alleged sympathy for the terrorist group Hamas and insisted instead that he just wanted to make life more affordable for the struggling citizens of his home state.

At rallies before Tuesday, El-Sayed stood behind the Stars and Stripes and said: ‘I love America like I love my children.’

In the early hours of Wednesday, however, with the result secured, he began his victory speech by chanting in Arabic.

An even more revealing statement came from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the far-Left Congresswoman who is expected to run for the presidency in 2028.

In August, a journalist asked ‘AOC’ about her ally, the Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong, who’d called for the ‘defunding’ of the police and the abolition of prisons.

‘I have a local city councilman that has this saying: “Woke 1 was crazy,” ’ she said. ‘And I think that what’s important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now.’

But she did not, crucially, say that Hong was wrong, and she did not admit the obvious implication: that Woke 2 can afford to be even crazier, if only its advocates avoid saying what they really think.

In fact, Woke 1 vs Woke 2 might be compared to the difference between Terminator 1 and Terminator 2. The new American socialism – and, make no mistake, it is socialist – is far more intelligent, potent and elusive. It can code-switch and even transform into a completely different creature in order to deceive the unsuspecting electorate and wrong-foot Maga Republicans.

In 2024, the Trump campaign produced a brilliantly simple and effective advertisement: ‘Kamala is for they/them,’ it said. ‘Donald Trump is for you.’ But Michigan Democrats snidely flipped that script. ‘The Republicans are for they/them,’ chortled the narrator as an image of Israel’s political leaders flashed on the screen. ‘Abdul El-Sayed is for you.’

In short, the far‑Left Democrats of 2026 have every intention of setting America in a new and very dangerous direction.

Which brings us back to Allison in Alabama. ‘People across the political spectrum seem to be making a big deal out of the trans thing’, the bespectacled individual said after winning. ‘I felt a calling to be a public servant, and now I’m gonna do my best for all of us, regardless of how you voted or what you think of my gender.’

Yet if anyone has made a big deal out of ‘the trans thing’, it is this 33-year-old, who testified against the What is a Woman Act, a piece of legislation which sought to recognise in law the biological nature of sex. Allison also opposed a Bill that would have restricted drag performances in schools.

Or just look at some of the other Democrats who enjoyed electoral victories this week.

Take Egyptian-born Adam Hamawy – and now New Jersey Congressman-elect – a plastic surgeon and former US Army medical officer who volunteered in Gaza. Reports have emerged that Hamawy was a close associate of Omar Abdel-Rahman – the ‘Blind Sheikh’ sentenced to life in prison for his role inspiring the 1993 World Trade Center bombing.

Court records show that Hamawy accompanied the Islamist cleric to a conference in Michigan, titled Towards A Global Islamic Economy in 1991, served as his translator during a press conference and testified on his behalf during his federal criminal trial.

There’s Ilhan Omar, who just won re-election in Minnesota, even though the Justice Department is investigating her for marrying a man who could allegedly be her brother. Last month, a journalist asked Omar if she was ‘in any way’ related to her second husband, whom she divorced in 2017. ‘Not to my knowledge,’ she replied, alarmingly.

Omar, a close political ally of AOC, danced with her third husband at her election-night party this week and talked throughout the campaign about ‘Medicare for All’ and ‘economic justice’. But she’s also openly adamant that she wants to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), a once-fringe group, have emerged as an increasingly powerful force in US politics with a set of bizarre and extremist policies to match.

A recent DSA manifesto calls for the closure of all overseas US military bases, the stopping of all sanctions on Cuba, Venezuela and Iran, and ‘universal free housing’.

And now several new DSA-backed Democrats are going to Congress. There’s Gen Z Melat Kiros, who just won the first district of Colorado. She believes ICE is a ‘rogue paramilitary force’ and described the October 7 attacks on Israel as ‘the inevitable consequences of apartheid’.

There’s the equally delightful Darializa Avila Chevalier, ‘a working-class Dominican New Yorker’ who wants ‘a world without borders’ and reposted social media comments that Israel ‘doesn’t exist’. She’s an admirer of the late Assata Shakur, the Black Panther who, in 1977, was found guilty of murdering a state trooper.

And there’s Chris Rabb, in Philadelphia, who wants ‘nationalised grocery stores’ and calls America’s immigration detention facilities ‘concentration camps’. He rejects the idea that immigration can be illegal.

It’s all very extreme.

This week proved that Americans are sick of Trump Republicanism. The citizenry is craving a return to decency and common sense in public life.

But just wait until voters get to know some of the Democrats they just sent to Washington.

Freddy Gray is deputy editor of The Spectator and the editor of the US edition

news.title: Nithya Raman wins LA mayoral race, becoming city’s first South Asian mayor  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily
news.text:
Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles City Council member, has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, putting her on track to become the first South Asian to lead the second largest city in the United States.

The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with Raman holding 52 percent of the vote.

Raman, 45, overtook Bass despite the incumbent’s support from prominent Democrats like California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with her victory coming as part of a surge in visibility and electoral wins for the left-wing political movement.

A record number of candidates backed or affiliated with the DSA won federal offices in Tuesday’s midterm elections. On its website, the DSA has claimed credit for contributing to at least 300 candidacies or ballot referendums during the midterms, and it said it is on track to count 105 of those as victories.

Some of those wins include congressional races, with figures like Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros and Chris Rabb winning their first terms as US representatives.

Raman’s victory in Los Angeles follows another high-profile democratic socialist winning a mayor’s race in New York City last year: Zohran Mamdani.

Raman was born in India and worked as an urban planner before running for office. Once an ally of Bass, she had initially endorsed her re-election campaign but reversed course, entering the mayoral race in February, just hours before the filing deadline.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she said to the crowd.

Raman also pledged to expand affordable housing, improve neglected city services and take a different approach to homelessness by deploying more medical teams to assist people who are unhoused.

In addition, she called for replacing the city’s police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Raman now faces the task of delivering on those promises in a city of more than 3.8 million people.

Los Angeles also faces the hurdle of hosting the 2028 Olympic Games, starting in July of that year.

With Thursday’s election results, Bass has become the first Los Angeles mayor in nearly two decades to lose a re-election bid.

Her defeat follows a difficult four years in office. Her administration faced mounting criticism over the city’s homelessness crisis and its response to the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was overseas and devastated communities across the Los Angeles area.

In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and added that she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.

“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me,” Bass wrote.

“Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”

news.title: New York’s 5 Costliest House Races Draw $308M in Spending
news.text:
New York congressional races drew a staggering $308 million in spending during the 2026 midterm campaign, including roughly $64 million in the Empire State’s most closely watched battleground.

The contest for New York’s suburban 17th Congressional District in the Hudson Valley generated $64 million between a fiercely contested Democratic primary and the general election. The total includes spending by candidates’ campaigns and political action committees.

About $22 million was spent during the Democratic primary, in which military veteran and eventual winner Cait Conley defeated Beth Davidson and Peter Chatzky, according to campaign finance records. Outside groups also poured $30 million into the swing district, which encompasses portions of Westchester, Dutchess, Rockland and Putnam counties, filings show.

On Tuesday, Conley unseated two-term incumbent Rep. Mike Lawler, who had won reelection in 2024 even as Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris carried the 17th District.

The spending pushed the race far beyond the $38.4 million spent in New York’s 19th Congressional District in 2024, which was then the most expensive general election contest on record.

Several high-profile New York City primaries also ranked among the year’s most expensive contests, including the Manhattan battle to replace retiring Rep. Jerry Nadler in the 12th District.

Democratic candidates and the groups supporting them spent $56 million in that race, records show. Super PACs, including Jobs and Democracy PAC and Think Big, accounted for the bulk of the spending, with $43 million invested in the contest.

Those groups received substantial backing from artificial intelligence companies and their leaders, who spent heavily in the June primary as concerns about the emerging technology resonated with Democratic voters. Democrat Micah Lasher ultimately won both the primary and the general election.

The race to succeed North Country Rep. Elise Stefanik in the 21st District was the third-most expensive overall. It included a bitter primary between eventual Republican nominee Anthony Constantino and GOP Assemblyman Robert Smullen.

Constantino went on to win a nail-biting general election against Democratic dairy farmer Blake Gendebien, despite Stefanik carrying the district by more than 20 points in each of the previous two cycles.

The Democratic-aligned House Majority PAC made a seven-figure advertising buy in the week before Election Day. Constantino, an Amsterdam-based chief executive of a sticker and decal manufacturing company, meanwhile invested $17 million of his own fortune in the race.

Democratic socialist star Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez faced no serious reelection challenge in the 14th Congressional District, but $26 million was still spent on the contest, making it New York’s fourth-most expensive House race.

Ocasio-Cortez, who is openly considering a presidential or Senate bid in 2028, had $18 million cash on hand as of mid-October.

The fifth-most expensive contest was the $20 million showdown in New York’s 3rd Congressional District between Rep. Tom Suozzi, D-N.Y., and former Assemblyman Mike LiPetri, records show.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, like Ocasio-Cortez, faced no competitive challenge but still spent $19 million, according to filings.

Left-wing Democratic socialist challenger Darializa Aviles-Chevalier’s primary defeat of Rep. Adriano Espaillat in the 13th District ranked as the seventh-most expensive race, with approximately $15.4 million spent, records show.

news.title: Nithya Raman wins LA mayoral race, becoming city’s first South Asian mayor
news.text:
Nithya Raman, a progressive Los Angeles City Council member, has defeated incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, putting her on track to become the first South Asian to lead the second-largest city in the United States.

The Associated Press called the race for Raman on Thursday, with Raman holding 52 percent of the vote.

Raman, 45, overtook Bass despite the incumbent’s support from prominent Democrats such as California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

Her campaign was backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), with her victory coming as part of a surge in visibility and electoral wins for the left-wing political movement.

A record number of candidates backed or affiliated with the DSA won federal offices in Tuesday’s midterm elections. On its website, the DSA has claimed credit for contributing to at least 300 candidacies or ballot referendums during the midterms, and it said it is on track to count 105 of those as victories.

Some of those wins came in congressional races, with figures such as Darializa Avila Chevalier, Claire Valdez, Melat Kiros and Chris Rabb winning their first terms as US representatives.

Raman’s victory in Los Angeles follows another high-profile democratic socialist winning a mayor’s race in New York City last year: Zohran Mamdani.

Raman was born in India and worked as an urban planner before running for office. Once an ally of Bass, she had initially endorsed her re-election campaign but reversed course, entering the mayoral race in February, just hours before the filing deadline.

In her victory speech, Raman promised to restore what she called an ambitious, creative and entrepreneurial Los Angeles.

“For too long our broken and unjust status quo has convinced Angelenos that this is the best that we can do,” she told the crowd.

Raman also pledged to expand affordable housing, improve neglected city services and take a different approach to homelessness by deploying more medical teams to assist people who are unhoused.

In addition, she called for replacing the city’s police chief over concerns about cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

Raman now faces the task of delivering on those promises in a city of more than 3.8 million people.

Los Angeles also faces the challenge of hosting the 2028 Olympic Games, which open in July of that year.

With the result, Bass has become the first Los Angeles mayor in more than two decades to lose a re-election bid.

Her defeat follows a difficult four years in office. Her administration faced mounting criticism over the city’s homelessness crisis and its response to the deadly Palisades Fire, which broke out while she was overseas and devastated communities across the Los Angeles area.

In a statement on Thursday, Bass congratulated Raman and said she was committed to ensuring a smooth transition.

“Four years ago, you elected me as the first Black woman mayor in the history of Los Angeles. You gave me the honor of serving the city that raised me, and every single day since, I have carried that responsibility with me,” Bass wrote.

“Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us.”
news.summary: DSA-backed Raman will lead the second-largest US city, promising action on homelessness and affordable housing.

news.title: Mississippi, Alaska Senate Races Remain Too Close to Call
news.text:
Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain too close to call as Democratic challengers cling to slim leads.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom has a narrow lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, an unexpected development in a reliably red state.

The razor-thin margin surprised political experts as Mississippi has long been a Republican stronghold. It came alongside other surprising Democratic wins in the American South.

Alaska’s Senate race also remains unresolved, with Democratic challenger Mary Peltola hanging on to a 637-vote lead over Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan, according to The Associated Press, with 74 percent of ballots counted.

As of Nov. 5, Colom held a 1,145-vote lead on Hyde-Smith, according to the Associated Press, with 96 percent of the vote counted.

That’s in a state President Donald Trump won in 2024 with 60.9 percent of the vote, defeating Kamala Harris by 22.9 points. Hyde-Smith won reelection in 2020 over Democratic challenger Mike Espy by a 54 percent–44 percent margin.

Matthew Dallek, a political science professor at George Washington University, told The Epoch Times that the economy, the war in Iran, and high gas and grocery prices contributed to the tight race.

Dallek said the switch was a perfect storm where black voters supported Democratic candidates in Mississippi while Latino voters came out in full force to elect Democrats in Texas after members of the two demographics helped elect Trump in 2024.

“So this is true across the South. Like, very large African American turnout, which is part of a response to the gutting of the Voting Rights Act and a response to maybe Trump gutting affirmative action and all kinds of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives and civil rights measures,” Dallek said.

He was referring to the U.S. Supreme Court’s ruling on the Voting Rights Act and gerrymandering in April. A majority said Louisiana’s Senate Bill 8, which created a second majority-black district, was racial gerrymandering and unconstitutional. Critics, however, warned it would have far-reaching impacts for voting rights.

University of South Florida political science professor J. Edwin Benton told The Epoch Times that southern voters were once part of a “solid Democratic South” before a shift to conservatism in the 1980s and 1990s in the Deep South and Florida.

The rise of Trump and the Make America Great Again movement solidified Republican support in states such as Mississippi and South Carolina.

The midterms changed the political alignment, with Democrats making gains in traditional Republican states, including Texas, Iowa, and Kansas.

Benton said voters who were once captivated by Trump turned out in force due to the rising cost of gas prices and groceries and being at war.

Vice President JD Vance posted on X that low voter turnout was not the problem, saying many people who voted for Trump and Vance in 2024 turned to Democrats in 2026. He said the war in Iran, the cost of living, putting America first and the change in relationship with Israel were the reasons Republicans lost.

In Florida’s 14th Congressional District, longtime Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor fended off Republican challenger Mike Beltran.

Despite a redrawn district, Benton said Castor won because she has delivered on promises over her nearly 20 years in office.

The Alaska Senate Race has proven to be tighter than Mississippi’s, as Peltola has a slim lead over Sullivan in another state controlled by Republicans.

In Alaska, if neither candidate gets 50 percent or more of the votes, rules call for a ranked-choice tabulation, where voters would rank their choice in order of preference.

The trending results are a far cry from the incumbent Sullivan’s previous run in 2020, when he won his second term by more than 12 points over nonpartisan candidate Al Gross.

But Peltola has proven to be a formidable challenger as votes continued to be counted in a normally Republican-controlled state.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit to segregate and review ballots cast for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan, asserting that his appearance on the ballot created confusion with Sen. Dan Sullivan.
news.summary: Other surprising wins have emerged in the American South.
news.author: Craig Shoup
